abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) errors on visual reasoning may come from missing visual structure, from mistakes after that structure is extracted, or from both. We introduce VRIQ, a benchmark of 1,391 human-verified IQ-style visual reasoning puzzles spanning five psychometric categories, each instantiated in category-matched abstract and natural-image domains. To study perception and reasoning more directly, we also introduce DiagVRIQ, a 209-item diagnostic subset paired with human-verified, rule-neutral textual descriptions. Across 21 VLMs, the 17 non-frontier models reach a 26.8% unweighted category mean on abstract puzzles, while three 2026 frontier models improve substantially but unevenly, with unweighted category means of 41.3--70.9% on abstract puzzles and at most 78.2% on natural-image puzzles; all remain below human performance. On DiagVRIQ, even when their descriptions are judged correct, the strongest models still answer approximately 9--12% of those items incorrectly. Two interventions, ground-truth description augmentation and tool-augmented inference, improve accuracy, with the largest tool gains on spatially demanding categories, but neither eliminates errors. VRIQ and DiagVRIQ provide a framework for studying visual reasoning through complementary end-to-end, description-based, and intervention-based analyses rather than treating it as a single monolithic capability.

title: Causal Front-Door Adjustment for Robust Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs
justification: Jailbreak attack method, not inference serving.
hype_justification: Jailbreak/safety is popular but this is a specialized white-box approach.
abstract: Jailbreak attacks on safety-aligned LLMs are increasingly effective, yet attack success alone does not reveal whether compliance is driven by preserved task intent, suppressed safety signals, or attack-specific artifacts. We use Pearl's front-door adjustment to motivate separating task-relevant semantics from safety-related variation. We propose Causal Front-Door Adjustment Attack (CFA^2), a white-box framework that operationalizes this perspective in LLM latent space using Sparse Autoencoders, contrastive datasets, and weight orthogonalization. After offline calibration, CFA^2 enables efficient generation without per-prompt iterative optimization, performs strongly on HarmBench across four open-source LLMs, and provides source-side signals for same-family black-box prompt transfer.

title: Rethinking Floorplan Generation with Space Syntax: From Design Theory to Model Improvement
justification: Floorplan generation with space syntax, unrelated.
abstract: Architectural design increasingly adopts generative AI (GenAI) for floorplan generation, an early-stage design task exploring how spaces should be organized for use. Yet fidelity objectives inherited from native visual and geometric generators do not automatically capture this design purpose. This organization remains largely implicit in generated representations, limiting direct evaluation and feedback. Drawing on space syntax, an established architectural design theory, the Space Syntax Integration Operator (SSIO) recovers convex-space access graphs across heterogeneous formats. This theory-grounded shared intermediate representation, which we call a design container, supports evaluation and model understanding of spatial design. Applying SSIO to four residential corpora spanning 15 countries reveals public spaces' integration levels are highest, with corpus-dependent distributions. These patterns underpin the RPLAN-SSI benchmark, an empirical design reference system assessing population-level functional-profile alignment (IPD) and within-plan public-space advantage (PIA). Comparison with this residential reference reveals a design gap: public spaces in generated floorplans have a smaller integration advantage over other spaces. To address this gap, Space Syntax-Guided Post-Training (SSPT) provides a plug-and-play design-learning interface: SSIO-derived RL feedback improves IPD and PIA across five heterogeneous diffusion backbones while preserving native mechanisms. We further discuss how this approach may inform GenAI applications in other design domains.

title: Structural Pass Analysis in Football: Learning Pass Archetypes and Tactical Impact from Spatio-Temporal Tracking Data
justification: Football pass analytics from tracking data, unrelated.
abstract: Football action-value approaches estimate scoring, possession, or other downstream outcome value; complementary descriptions can characterise how a pass relates to the opposition's spatial structure. We introduce an interpretable structural-passing framework using tracking and event information, with three descriptors: Line Bypass Score (LBS), a signed difference in opponents remaining goal-side between passer and receiver coordinates; Space Gain Metric (SGM), relative nearest-opponent distance at the receiver versus a floored passer reference; and Structural Disruption Index (SDI), aggregate differences in defensive-shape summaries between pass time and the nearest sampled state one second later. The metrics are transformed and standardised before combination in Tactical Impact Value (TIV), a fixed-weight structural composite. We apply the framework to 41,078 open-play pass events with identified passer and receiver from the 2022 FIFA World Cup. The selected K=4 partition provides an interpretable operational taxonomy of four profiles: Circulatory, Destabilising, Line-breaking, and Space-expanding. The profiles show different structural metric signatures, and the reported territorial-crossing and stored outcome indicators vary descriptively across profiles and TIV strata. Team, spatial, player, and passer--receiver analyses illustrate how the structural representation can be summarised at multiple levels. The findings position the framework as a complement to outcome-oriented action-value analysis, offering football analysts interpretable structural evidence to support tactical interpretation and guide further investigation.

title: GAC: Noise-Aware Adaptive Mixing for Hybrid SFT-RL Post-Training
justification: Hybrid SFT-RL post-training mixing, a training-alignment method.
hype_justification: Post-training recipe with released Qwen checkpoint; some practitioner interest.
abstract: Hybrid post-training combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) is the standard paradigm for aligning large language models, yet fixed mixing schedules cannot adapt when the relative noise of the two signals evolves. We derive a noise-aware mixing weight mu* by minimizing an MSE upper bound on the mixed stochastic gradient, yielding a closed-form that balances gradient noise variance and SFT-RL disagreement. Building on the token-wise reweighting of CHORD, the practical Guided Adaptive Controller (GAC) adds EMA smoothing, a schedule prior, and capped updates around this estimator, with all statistics estimated online from existing training tensors. The noise-aware controller alone outperforms the best rule-based controller by +3.0 percentage points on AMC; the full system reaches +3.8 points over HPT across math, code, science, and logic benchmarks, while reducing KL-drift area by 28% and large absolute mixing-weight changes by more than 70%, at less than 1% overhead. Gains grow with model size from 1.5B to 14B. Resources: Qwen3.5-4B compact-backbone release: https://huggingface.co/YueLinHu/GAC-Qwen3.5-4B; reference implementation: https://github.com/deepnovacore/GAC; GAC project page: https://deepnovacore.github.io/GAC/

title: How Much Can Repeated Running Buy? A Measured Variance Ceiling for LLM Code Evaluation
justification: Statistical analysis of benchmark variance for code eval, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Methodological evaluation critique; niche but cited by eval-focused readers.
abstract: A benchmark score is a measurement whose uncertainty has two sources: an aleatoric component from stochastic decoding and an epistemic component from the finite problem set. Using 16 models on 99 recent LeetCode-style problems with two prompts and five runs each (15,840 judged runs in a fully crossed design), we estimate both components and ask a design question: how much can repeated running buy? First, the pooled-binomial interval that repeated-run protocols invite answers neither question of interest---it is about $2\times$ too narrow for generalisation to new problems and $2\times$ too wide for the fixed problem set---and under correctly clustered intervals, 12 of 15 adjacent leaderboard pairs are statistically unresolved. Second, the variance ceiling $1+μ_w/σ_b^2$, the largest factor by which repetition can reduce score variance, has median 1.34 across models (range 1.05--1.71), so repetition can narrow confidence intervals by at most 23% on this benchmark, and by 14% for the median model. Third, once the cost of adding verified problems is priced in, the precision-optimal repeat count is $R^{*}=\sqrt{μ_w c_p/(σ_b^2 c_g)}$, and the variance curve is flat around it: on this benchmark the decisive reason to repeat is not precision but identification---two to three runs suffice to estimate the components that the ceiling and the fixed-benchmark interval require. All three are measurements of one benchmark at one decoding temperature, and we state explicitly what they do and do not license.

title: ThreadBench: Benchmarking Realism in Agentic Simulation of Real-world Discussions
justification: Reddit discussion simulation benchmark, not inference.
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used to simulate real-world interactions, but it remains unclear whether simulated behaviors preserve the content patterns and interaction dynamics of real human behaviors. Existing evaluations often focus on individual comments or task performance, rather than whether simulated behaviors match human behavior at thread level. In this paper, we use Reddit discussions as a concrete testbed for real-world social simulation. Reddit provides public, topic-grounded, multi-party interactions with diverse opinions, experiences, and interaction patterns, making it a useful setting for evaluating whether LLM agents reproduce the distributional and structural properties of real online discussions. We introduce ThreadBench, a benchmark for Reddit discussion simulation built from 9,817 real Reddit threads spanning 8 diverse domains and 116 subdomains. ThreadBench uses statistical analyses to compare generated and real discussions across 12 metrics grouped in 4 families: uniformity, expression, tone, and interaction. We further develop Thread-Prompt-based Discussion Generation (ThreadPDG), a Planner-Writer framework that learns how a real discussion grows. The Planner produces thread- and comment-level plans from a real seed discussion, and the Writer generates comments from these plans. For each seed, we generate multiple candidate threads and combine their best branches using thread-level statistics. Across all domains and multiple LLMs, ThreadPDG achieves ThreadBench pass rates of 58-100%, compared with 0-17% for the baselines. Human evaluation with 436 annotators further shows that ThreadPDG is not distinguished from real discussions in 78.7% of pairs, outperforming existing simulation methods.

title: DBA-Bench: A Production-Fidelity Benchmark for LLM-Based Database Operations Agents
justification: Database operations agent benchmark, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Agentic DB benchmark on live systems; agents are trendy.
abstract: LLM-based database agents show promise, but differences in task scope, testbeds, and success criteria hinder direct comparison. A shared benchmark must also preserve the operational conditions that determine whether diagnosis and remediation succeed in practice. We present DBA-Bench, guided by operational realism, outcome-first evaluation, and controlled scenario reproducibility. It evaluates agents in live PostgreSQL and distributed TiDB deployments with active workloads, stateful behavior, and multi-source observations. Success requires satisfying scenario-specific operational objectives without violating safety constraints. The primary evaluation covers 231 bounded scenarios across five operational domains, while 10 persistent scenarios extend evaluation to continued operation across interacting events. We evaluate eight automated baselines, including four frontier foundation models, two open-weight models, and two GPT-5.5-backed database agents. Our evaluation exposes gaps between diagnosis, effective remediation, and safe execution across both database systems. Agents can identify root causes yet fail to restore operational objectives. Even when objectives are restored, the executed actions can violate safety constraints. Persistent scenarios expose a gap between clearing individual blockers and sustaining business service: agents leave competing workloads uncoordinated and previously completed repairs unchecked after subsequent changes.

title: Need or Reputation? Region, National Income, and Academic Status in LLM Gatekeeping Decisions
justification: LLM gatekeeping fairness study, unrelated to inference.
abstract: Equitable access to scientific knowledge often depends on informal gatekeeping decisions, particularly when resources such as paywalled articles, nonpublic datasets, or a researcher's CV must be shared selectively. We introduce a controlled simulation framework in which LLM-based professors must grant access to only one requester. Across prompts, requesters vary systematically by global region (Global North vs. Global South) and academic seniority, while all other factors remain constant. Most models prioritize PhD candidates, although preferences vary by model and scenario (e.g., Claude favors tenured professors when the request is for the professor's CV), and the smaller models' status choices are sensitive to the order in which options are presented. When the requesters' regions differ, the models split into two groups. The three large proprietary LLMs systematically favor requesters from the Global South, a pro-equity bias consistent with their safety alignment, whereas the two small open-weight models reverse this preference and favor the Global North, possibly reflecting weaker alignment or the geographic skew of their pre-training data. Linking choices to national income reveals that the large models' preference largely tracks economic need rather than the regional label: they strongly favor requesters from low-income countries, but their preference for the Global South is weak or absent when both countries have equal income, whereas the small models favor the Global North regardless of income. Because model scale, alignment, and training data are confounded in our sample, these explanations remain hypotheses for future work. Our findings show that LLMs embed differing normative assumptions about need and reputation that can shape gatekeeping decisions, which highlights the need to audit AI systems for fairness and value alignment before such tasks are delegated to them.

title: Plausible but Not Valid: A Psychometric Audit of LLMs as Synthetic Survey Respondents
justification: Psychometric audit of LLMs as survey respondents, not inference.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as synthetic survey respondents, but existing evaluations mostly ask whether individual answers look plausible. We ask a stricter, psychometric question: do LLMs preserve the joint distribution, latent structure, reliability, mediation pathways, and demographic effects of real human survey data? We introduce an open Lithuanian organisational-psychology dataset (n=263 employees; three validated instruments; 68 items, 12 subscales) and condition 37 LLMs on real respondent profiles under a persona-disclosure ladder, presentation, reasoning-effort and cross-language ablations, counterfactual demographic swaps, and a memorization probe. The resulting Psychometric Similarity Score (PSS) is anchored against five statistical baselines, a held-out human ceiling, and the real answers of the same respondents. LLMs reproduce the direction of human psychometric relationships, but statistical baselines with no language model match or beat them. The best LLM (PSS 0.81) is level with a Gaussian copula fit only on other respondents (0.82) and below the real answers of the same 100 people (0.89). A simple classifier separates every LLM sample from humans (median AUC 0.99), and verbatim recall of the items is rare (at most 4.7%) and unrelated to PSS. Counterfactual swaps move answers in the direction of human group differences and by a similar amount (role 0.49 and education 0.33 human SD, vs. 0.46 and 0.44 in humans). Gender swaps move them by 0.06 SD. Tucker's phi on UWES falls inside an item-permutation null for 10 of 37 models. Synthetic respondents compress the response scale (within-respondent SD 0.79 vs. 1.19), lose predictive validity on held-out humans (mean R^2=-0.14 vs. 0.28), and produce significant indirect effects on 4 of 7 mediation paths that are null in humans. LLM samples are therefore not a drop-in replacement for human survey data.

title: Time as Structure: Temporal Dependency Graphs for Verifiable Deadline Computation over Legal Documents
justification: Legal deadline computation pipeline, not inference systems.
abstract: Miss a filing deadline by one day and the claim is barred, however strong the case. Computing that deadline is rarely simple: the period runs from a triggering event, is counted by a statutory convention, and may be suspended by a mandatory conciliation window. We ask whether a language model should answer such questions directly, or read the document and leave the arithmetic to code. We extract dated facts and their dependencies into a temporal dependency graph and compute deadlines from it with a calendar-correct engine. On UK Employment Appeal Tribunal judgments the engine reproduces six of seven timeliness rulings, and matches the judges' own dates to the day. The strongest of four language models, asked the same cases, gets the arithmetic right and the answer wrong: in two of its seven responses its stated verdict contradicts its own working, and across the three GPT models six of twenty-one responses do, each time calling a late claim timely. To test the systems at scale we move the dismissal date across the statutory boundary, generating 427 cases whose answers are computed rather than annotated. On the cases both systems answer, the pipeline is right 90.2% of the time against 61.2% for direct answering. It answers two thirds of the cases, and counting its abstentions as errors it does not exceed direct answering (60.4% against 64.6%). The limit is extraction: on contracts the errors are almost never in the arithmetic, but in choosing which event the period starts from.

title: SIDScope: A Diagnostic Resource for Semantic-ID Interfaces in Generative Recommendation
justification: Semantic-ID diagnostics for generative recommendation, not inference serving.
abstract: Semantic ID tokenizers assign code sequences to catalog items, which generative recommenders predict and resolve back to items. Reusing a released mapping requires checking its code organization, item resolution, and compatibility with an existing model after a refresh. SIDScope provides these checks through source traced adapters, mapping diagnostics, candidate retrieval tests, and generated trace analysis. Its inventory contains nine exports from seven tokenizer families across Amazon and Yelp, including eight executable routes and one auditable snapshot. The analyses establish three distinctions. First, code allocation and item addressability differ: in GRID, tail items occupy 95.7 distinct codes per 100 items, yet only 82.2 percent have globally unique codes. Second, prefix alignment calibrates retrieval operations that use prefixes. With fixed candidate budgets and ranking, original assignments on Beauty and Instruments expose more targets than controls preserving code capacity and coarse popularity. Resolving identical generated paths also shows that an explicit item selection rule recovers part of the gap between target path survival and singleton credit. Third, a released refresh repairs missing codes, while model adaptation separately restores new item recall. SIDScope supplies code, diagnostic summaries, and verification tools to compare mappings, evaluate their use in retrieval and generation, and test model reuse after changes.

title: Dense Weak Hiding: Closing Complexity Gaps in Nonconvex and PL Finite-Sum Optimization under Individual Smoothness
justification: Optimization complexity lower bounds theory, unrelated.
abstract: Under individual smoothness, known algorithms for nonconvex finite-sum optimization use $O(n+\sqrt nΔL_{\max}/\varepsilon^2)$ incremental first-order oracle (IFO) calls, while existing lower bounds miss the factor $\sqrt n$ in the second term. We prove the matching lower bound $Ω(n+\sqrt nΔL_{\max}/\varepsilon^2)$ for randomized IFO algorithms, allowing component indices and query points to depend on the complete preceding history. Thus PAGE and SPIDER are minimax optimal up to universal constants under individual and mean-squared smoothness. Under the global Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition, prior lower bounds did not capture the correct dependence on $n$ under individual smoothness, and the regime of small $κ$ remained open for randomized IFO algorithms. We prove an $Ω(n+κ_{\max}\sqrt n\log(Δ/\varepsilon))$ lower bound for $κ_{\max}\ge\sqrt n$, and an $Ω(n+n\log(Δ/\varepsilon)/(1+\log(\sqrt n/κ_{\max})))$ lower bound for $3\leκ_{\max}\le\sqrt n$. Restarted PAGE attains matching upper bounds under mean-squared smoothness in terms of $κ_{\rm ms}=L_{\rm ms}/μ$. Our lower bounds use dense weak hiding. Each hidden direction is spread across all components, making individual queries weakly informative while preserving the direction in the average. A sufficiently large dimension makes premature activation of future stages unlikely within the query budget. Balancing the cost of revealing a stage against the number of stages permitted by individual smoothness yields the missing $\sqrt n$ factor.

title: Evaluating and Recalibrating Probabilistic Classifiers from One-Bit Threshold Queries
justification: Calibration from one-bit threshold queries; LLM logit_bias instantiation is tangential.
abstract: Standard calibration evaluation and recalibration methods assume access to predicted probabilities. We study one-bit threshold access, a setting in which probabilities are hidden and the evaluator observes only whether the predicted probability exceeds a single chosen threshold per sample. Under this restriction, we show that classifiers can nevertheless be evaluated and recalibrated without reconstructing their hidden scores. We derive a consistent estimator of True Calibration Error, unbiased estimators of strictly proper scoring rules, and a one-bit objective for Temperature Scaling whose expectation matches the standard log-loss objective. Across these settings, we quantify the statistical cost incurred by replacing standard probability-access procedures by our one-bit estimators. Finally, we instantiate the framework for black-box LLMs, where the logit_bias API parameter allows us to realize the required threshold queries in zero-shot binary question answering.

title: A BUD You Can Count On: Efficient, Verifiable Membership Proofs
justification: Blockchain membership-proof structures, unrelated.
abstract: A block typically changes only a small fraction of blockchain state, yet producing a state root makes validators update an authenticated tree spanning it all. We show how to support verifiable reads from the writes alone. We introduce Block Update Digests (BUDs), that commit to a block's writes and link each key touched in that block to its previous modification. An optional prior-value record lets one successor BUD authenticate the value between modifications, replacing the baseline's two BUD openings. SuperBUDs summarize those writes over longer intervals, letting a reader verify that a value remained unchanged without checking every intervening block. Thanks to BUDs and SuperBUDs, validators can just keep ordinary flat state while still serving proofs of current and historical values, including deletion. We prove soundness and completeness for reads at or after a key's first logged modification when the required proof data is available. In experiments with the baseline format, a 50x increase in state size raises the measured base-BUD cost by just 1.24x. In paired QMDB experiments, lowering its garbage-collection activation threshold raises process CPU time by 1.3-2.7x and device bytes written by 1.6-2.4x relative to its dormant configuration. BUD authentication requires no corresponding relocation of live entries. In the evaluated baseline, two-digest read-layer payloads stay below 800 bytes, and warm hash-path verification takes at most 146 μs at p99. Authenticated reads need not make validators maintain an authenticated tree over the entire state.

title: CataOPD: Catalytic On-Policy Distillation for Large Language Model Reasoning
justification: On-policy distillation for reasoning, a training method.
hype_justification: RL/distillation for reasoning is hot; code released.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD) are two representative paradigms for improving large language model reasoning. However, when no correct trajectory is sampled, RL lacks a positive correctness signal, while OPD remains constrained by the reasoning trajectories reachable under the student's on-policy distribution. Therefore, we propose CataOPD, where the teacher acts as a catalyst rather than a target, expanding reachability while internalizing verified student-produced trajectories into a catalyst-free policy. Self-Rescue Routing uses empirically all-failed groups as routing signals rather than teacher-intervention triggers, first seeking correct trajectories through additional on-policy self-sampling. For problems unresolved after self-rescue, Catalytic-Guided Self-Resolution uses catalytic guidance to elicit a verified student-produced trajectory in the guided student distribution. Barrier-Weighted Internalization weights tokens by guided-to-unguided log-probability gaps, focusing updates on decisive tokens difficult without guidance. Experimental results show that CataOPD outperforms current baselines, extends independent student reasoning to still-unrecovered problems, and improves out-of-distribution generalization under catalyst-free inference. Our project is available at https://github.com/QwenQKing/CataOPD.

title: Are We Recovering Mechanisms? Objective-Level Recovery Gaps in Mechanistic Interpretability
justification: Mechanistic interpretability evaluation, not inference.
hype_justification: Interpretability is trendy and this challenges circuit-eval methodology.
abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to recover the internal computations responsible for model behavior. Progress in automated circuit discovery is often framed as a search problem: better attribution or optimization should identify better mechanisms. This assumes that the evaluation objective can recognize a better circuit once it is found. Yet standard intervention-based evaluation replaces signals outside a circuit to isolate its effect, changing the computational environment in which the retained components operate. We call this change context distortion. This raises the question of whether faithfulness rewards recovery of model behavior or compatibility with the altered context. We show that intervention-based faithfulness can prefer an equally sized circuit that reproduces the model's behavior less well. We call this reversal misranking, an objective-level recovery gap. To isolate evaluation from discovery, we construct equally sized candidates through controlled edits to human-identified circuits in pretrained language models, including IOI and Greater-Than, and benchmark circuits with known mechanisms. We find misranking even without a discovery algorithm. Misranking also occurs in real automated circuit-discovery settings. Among outputs of EAP, EAP-IG, ACDC, and Edge-SP, KL faithfulness under ordinary resampling prefers the behaviorally worse candidate in 13.2%-24.4% of candidate pairs across these methods on four pretrained-language-model tasks. Finally, restoring selected intact-model signals reverses 96 of 100 selected persistent misrankings, demonstrating that context distortion contributes to these failures. In light of these findings, we call for rethinking both how circuit discovery is performed and how its results are evaluated.

title: One Distribution, Two Channels: Coverage-Calibrated KV Retention and Compensation
justification: KV cache retention/eviction with coverage calibration for long-context decoding—core inference optimization.
hype_justification: KV cache compression is a hot topic; strong RULER/LongBench results likely to draw interest.
abstract: Long-context decoding is increasingly constrained by key--value (KV) cache memory and bandwidth. Existing fixed-budget compression methods typically separate retention from compensation, while a retention ranking specifies neither discarded attention mass nor the direction of induced output error. We start from an exact factorization: eviction error equals evicted attention mass times the directional gap between the evicted centroid and retained output, highlighting the importance of set-level coverage in retention and mass-preserving memory writing. We introduce CORE COverage Calibration and Evicted-Mass REdistribution for KV Cache, which distills an offline allocation combining query utility and log-determinant coverage into a lightweight cache-aware indexer. At inference, one calibrated distribution drives both channels: its Top-$B$ ordering retains complementary KV states, while its excluded allocation mass and conditional weights parameterize latent-memory writes without a separate write-weight predictor or online log-determinant evaluation. Our analysis provides a four-term pre-compensation error certificate, characterizes non-additive coverage interactions, and establishes mass-independent write stability with hierarchical bounds through recurrent and query-adaptive normalization. Across three backbones, CORE exceeds the strongest RULER baseline by up to 3.78 points at 90% compression; LongBench and repeated-eviction evaluations further demonstrate strong effectiveness and decoding efficiency.

title: Reference-Preserving Speculative Decoding on Consumer Systems: Diagnosis, Repair Scope, and Measured Cost
justification: Reference-preserving speculative decoding on quantized consumer runtimes—directly inference optimization.
hype_justification: Narrow single-author hardware-specific study despite hot speculative-decoding topic.
abstract: Speculative decoding changes the numerical history of a quantized runtime as well as its execution cost. When an application requires a fixed ordinary greedy output, the runtime must establish where constraints are needed and whether the qualified design saves time. We connect local state/path diagnosis, phase-scoped repair and measured comparisons with ordinary and matched target-only execution. Natural donor-state crosses on CUDA and Vulkan distinguish current-path, retained-state and interaction effects; a separate B570 fork study shows that immediate agreement can coexist with later divergence. On RTX, a query-layout transformation retains batched projection and feed-forward work. Target prefill and continuation form an inclusion-minimal passing set within a tested four-switch family, and the frozen design qualifies full responses on 24 project-unused inputs. Resident-request speed is 1.742 times ordinary execution; the matched draft-free path already achieves 1.683 times, leaving a 1.035-times speculative increment. Seven tasks regress against matched request time, and one round reverses direction. Wider fixed-capacity drafting and a B570 endpoint repair qualify while losing performance. Auxiliary M4 and 358H cases bound the value of added control and draft-only optimization. These results support a configuration-specific decision process from diagnosis through qualification to cost comparison; repair evidence remains restricted to the tested Qwen3 family.

title: Coarse-Graining Recursive Expert Computation: Continuation-Relative Interfaces and Failure Modes
justification: Computational coarse-graining of expert layers touches inference cost but is an abstract interface framework.
hype_justification: Abstract and hard-to-parse; limited practical uptake expected.
abstract: Computational coarse-graining aims to replace a sequence of updates with a cheaper module while preserving task performance. We present a continuation-relative evaluation framework that assesses replacements through the computation that follows them, using downstream task quality and total execution cost as joint criteria. The framework distinguishes boundary representations, summaries of skipped computation, executed operations, and downstream loss. It makes interfaces and permitted deployment information explicit, combines fine-path references with directly trained controls using the same shortened architecture, and accounts for selection overhead. An exact loss decomposition separates replacement effects at a fixed downstream action from effects of changing that action. A finite construction shows how retained information can reduce the stipulated cost of zero-error prediction under fixed information and controller restrictions. Experiments in two frozen pretrained language models show that representation fidelity and task loss can favor different fitting objectives. In a prespecified comparison on a 1.7-billion-parameter model, next-token-loss training lowers in-distribution negative log-likelihood by 0.1901 nats per scored token compared with reconstructing the skipped blocks' output, using the same optimizer and update count. This ranking reverses in all nine paired comparisons under distribution shift. In a recursive expert prototype, the jointly adapted candidate lowers task error relative to frozen-bank and router-only baselines, but trails directly trained controls, and the tested input-only selectors fail the joint quality-cost criteria. Together, the protocol and studies provide explicit criteria and diagnostics for distinguishing useful computational replacement from local approximation gains within specified interfaces and evaluation settings.

title: Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures
justification: Multimodal data-mixing scaling laws are pretraining-focused, not inference.
hype_justification: Big-name authors (Zettlemoyer, Bosselut), MoE scaling laws, hot topic—likely high attention.
abstract: Frontier AI systems are increasingly natively multimodal, jointly pretrained on multiple modalities, such as text, vision, and audio. However, the scientific understanding of the multimodal data mixtures used to pretrain these systems --- how much of each modality to mix, and at what potential interference cost to the others --- is largely absent or gatekept. In this work, we derive data mixing scaling laws for three modalities: text, vision, and audio. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, as MoEs scale efficiently and partially limit cross-modal interference. We therefore use MoEs to conduct 268 experiments ranging from 457M to 8.3B parameters, on up to 150 billion tokens. Our work leads to multiple actionable insights into multimodal data mixing for training MLLMs. First, compute optima are modality-specific: audio modality is model-heavy, favoring scaling parameters over tokens, while text and vision require balanced scaling of model size and data. Second, repeating vision or audio data beyond 2x yields negligible benefits. Finally, cross-modal interactions are highly asymmetric: vision strongly interferes with audio, whereas audio's interference with learning text and vision is negligible. Overall, we provide a principled foundation for understanding the multimodal data mixtures needed to train frontier MLLMs.

title: ByteMark: A Unified Byte-Level Watermark for Detection Across Language Models
justification: Byte-level text watermarking, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Watermarking is a deployment-relevant hot topic; cross-model angle is novel.
abstract: As watermarking of LLM-generated text enters deployment, users increasingly need to check text whose source is unknown. Existing detectors read the watermark through a specific tokenizer or embedding pipeline, and even if all providers adopted the same watermarking method, differences in these representations would leave their watermarks incompatible, and the text alone does not reveal which representation produced it. We propose ByteMark, a unified watermarking scheme that defines its signal on the UTF-8 bytes of published text. Models with different tokenizers embed this signal under one public specification and key, and a single detector verifies the text from the text and key alone. When the tokenizer or embedding model of a baseline detector is replaced, its detection degrades sharply, whereas ByteMark, which uses neither, retains its detection rate; ByteMark also remains detectable when participating models continue or rewrite the text.

title: Frustratingly Easy Agentic RAG via Portable Skills: A Case Study in Customer Support
justification: Agentic RAG via portable skills; mentions latency but is a RAG deployment case study, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Claude Code skills + agentic RAG are trendy; practical case study likely shared.
abstract: Enterprise workflow automation typically requires retrieving a complete and accurate set of relevant information from large operational document corpora (SOPs, policy documents) given a specific scenario or request. In customer support (CS), for example, human specialists must determine the correct sequence of resolution steps for each case, a task that demands precise grounding in policy documentation. Meeting this bar in production typically requires complex document chunking, indexing, and retrieval pipelines, often layered with learned re-rankers, query rewriters, and bespoke agentic RAG infrastructure. We report a deployment case study of a simpler alternative: a portable skill consisting of a natural-language instruction, lightweight tools (a retrieval API, format-checking scripts), and a corpus enriched with an LLM-generated navigation layer, which is a structured "Wikipedia-style" index over the underlying documents. This agentic RAG approach is straightforward to implement (1-2 engineer days), portable across capable agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code), and performs strongly on the challenging task of CS resolution workflow generation, achieving 99.2% procedural equivalence to human-approved ground truth and 83.3% evidence sufficiency. It is also roughly an order of magnitude slower per case than our deployed production assistant (~90 s vs. ~8-9 s), so we claim no latency advantage. Our claim is scoped to that setting: a mature, well-curated corpus, a latency-tolerant workflow, and human review of every case. There, the skill did the work of a complex RAG stack, and maintenance became a matter of editing text and data rather than retraining models.

title: MemForm: Benchmarking Memory Formation Poisoning in LLM Agents
justification: Memory-formation poisoning benchmark for agents, not inference.
hype_justification: Agent memory security is topical; benchmark release helps visibility.
abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM agents to learn from past interactions but exposes memory formation to adversarial influence. Existing studies primarily organize memory poisoning by attack channels, corruption patterns, or lifecycle stages, leaving formation interfaces insufficiently characterized. We formulate Memory Formation Poisoning as adversarial manipulation of the interfaces through which persistent agent memory is produced and committed, and introduce MemForm, a controlled diagnostic benchmark covering five interfaces: Content, Evidence, Scope, Selection, and Path Poisoning. We introduce Selection and Path Poisoning as controlled intervention categories that isolate retention and consolidation order effects, respectively. Each category pairs clean and poisoned conditions with interface-specific controls. Evaluations across six LLMs and two response formats reveal broad susceptibility at all five interfaces under the evaluated memory protocols and implementations. Crucially, authentic experiences with successful outcomes do not guarantee reliable behavior after memory formation: changes to contextual support, retention, or consolidation order can induce undesirable downstream behavior. In particular, consolidation order can alter behavior even with identical retained experiences, depending on the memory formation procedure. Additional analyses show that interface applicability depends on memory architecture and that Path Poisoning susceptibility depends on the updater. The evaluated defenses provide incomplete mitigation that varies by interface. These findings motivate protecting both what is committed to persistent memory and how memory is formed from experiences. Code and data are available at https://github.com/opanhw/memform-code.

title: Neither True nor False: Do LLMs Represent Truth-Value Gaps in Plural Predication?
justification: Semantic truth-value gaps in plural predication, unrelated.
abstract: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) genuinely grasp the truth conditions of plural descriptions, or do they force every sentence into true or false? We investigate the Homogeneity Gap, a semantic phenomenon where a plural definite (e.g., the kids laughed) and its negation (the kids didn't laugh) are both neither true nor false when only some of the kids laughed, whereas their quantified counterparts (all, not all) remain strictly bivalent. We introduce HomogeneityNLI, a diagnostic dataset of 1,000 minimal-pair items crossing determiner, polarity, and group composition across ten logical conditions. Evaluating seven open-weight models, we uncover a pervasive Bivalence Bias: models assign plural definites their homogeneous truth conditions, reading the kids as all of them and the kids didn't as none of them, yet collapse the truth-value gap into falsity. In the zero-shot setting, no model recognizes the gap for both polarities in more than 15% of scenarios, and negated definites are judged False in 84% of cases. Explicit linguistic rules, chain-of-thought, and enumeration prompts produce unstable, model-specific effects that often entrench the bias. Taken together, our findings indicate that current open-weight LLMs have acquired the truth conditions of plural predication but not its trivalent logic.

title: Target-ESS Tempered Policy Optimization (TETPO): Smooth Variance Control via Bridge Importance Sampling
justification: Tempered policy optimization for off-policy RL post-training, not inference.
hype_justification: Async RL stabilization is topical among RLHF practitioners.
abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement-learning post-training of large language models is computationally efficient but inherently off-policy: the learner updates on rollouts generated by a stale policy, while correcting this mismatch requires importance weights that can be extremely heavy-tailed. A small number of trajectories may then dominate an update, collapsing the effective sample size (ESS) and increasing the variance and instability of the resulting gradient estimates. Existing stabilizers apply fixed interventions regardless of the realized severity of weight concentration, either discarding selected samples or reweighting them without adapting the correction strength. We introduce \emph{Target--ESS Tempered Policy Optimization} (TETPO), which replaces each importance weight $ρ$ by $ρ^α$ for a data-adaptive exponent $α\in[0,1]$: $α=1$ preserves the original importance weights, whereas $α=0$ assigns uniform coefficients. For each prompt group, TETPO selects the largest $α$ whose tempered weights satisfy a target ESS fraction $κ$, applying little tempering to healthy groups and stronger tempering when weight degeneracy is severe. At the population level, the tempered coefficients are exact importance weights for a geometric bridge between the sampler and learner policies. The exponent is efficiently found by one-dimensional bisection, while the resulting weights satisfy deterministic bounds on normalized-weight dispersion and weighted-gradient norm that are independent of policy drift, together with a fixed-$α$ bound on bridge-target discrepancy. Power tempering also introduces no explicit zero-weight mask. On mathematical-reasoning benchmarks under high staleness, TETPO outperforms strong on- and off-policy baselines.

title: Evaluating Semantic Relation Knowledge through Bidirectional Relation Prediction from Gloss Pairs
justification: Semantic relation knowledge evaluation, unrelated to inference.
abstract: Semantic relations organise word senses and are fundamental to lexical semantics. In order to evaluate semantic relation knowledge of large language models (LLMs), we propose a challenging task in which an LLM predicts the relation between two glosses (definitions of senses) presented in two different orders. The predictions for the two orders are evaluated for consistency with the symmetry or asymmetry of semantic relations. Our task is designed for both monolingual and cross-lingual evaluation, allowing us to examine whether relation knowledge remains accessible when the same senses are verbalised through glosses in different languages. We construct a dataset of 3,069 sense pairs, with each sense verbalised in English, Greek, Romanian, Turkish, and Japanese. Experiments with 17 LLMs in zero-shot and five-shot settings reveal generally poor performance. In each setting, only eight LLMs achieve a macro-averaged F1 score significantly above a random baseline, and only one (zero-shot) and two (five-shot) significantly outperform a neural baseline. In particular, LLMs often fail to generate bidirectionally consistent predictions for hypernymy and to make correct predictions for holonymy in either direction. Our results suggest limitations in current LLMs' semantic relation knowledge, both in identifying relations and in respecting asymmetry.

title: Specification-Based Testing of Large Language Models
justification: Specification-driven safety testing of LLMs, not inference systems.
hype_justification: References Claude Opus 4.8 / GPT-5.5 system cards; safety-eval angle may draw clicks.
abstract: Model cards, system cards, and safety reports increasingly document LLM safety behaviors, yet safety evaluations typically start from predefined benchmarks rather than asking which documented claims those benchmarks actually test. We introduce LEST (LLM Evaluation through Specification-driven Testing), a framework that treats documented safety claims as specifications for black-box testing. In LEST, each claim determines which benchmark prompt tests it and whether a Refuse-to-Comply transition, where a model refuses a prompt but complies with its mutated version, counts as evidence against it. LEST mutates these prompts to search for counterexamples, manually validates each candidate, and traces validated counterexamples back to the claims they contradict. We evaluate LEST using the system cards of Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 with 97 seed prompts from SORRY-Bench across Mental Health and Self-Harm, Harmful and Violent Content, and Fairness and Bias. Of 56 identified safety claims, 29 (51.8%) are prompt-testable, but only 17 (58.6%) are exercised by an applicable benchmark prompt. Both models refuse >95% of benchmark prompts. Evaluating 1,836 mutated prompts on both models reveals 312 candidate Refuse-to-Comply transitions flagged by automated response classifiers. However, human validation confirms only 19 (6.1%) as both intent-preserving and genuinely compliant, showing automated evaluation substantially overestimates behavioral failures. Tracing these 19 transitions back to the claims reveals counterexamples for 6 of 9 covered claims for which refusal is an applicable oracle. Our results show that benchmark prompts may not be sufficient to validate all documented LLM safety behavior, and automated failure detection requires manual validation. LEST provides end-to-end traceability from natural-language safety documentation to executable tests and human-validated counterexamples.

title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization
justification: INT4 KV cache quantization for faster async RLVR rollouts—KV cache quantization and inference throughput.
hype_justification: Combines hot topics (KV quantization + RL rollouts) with concrete speedups on Qwen3.
abstract: Asynchronous rollout improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by reducing under-utilization during long-tail generation. Sustained concurrency also concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps, increasing the KV workload per step. We characterize this \emph{KV concentration} and find that KV cache quantization delivers substantially greater acceleration than weight-only and weight-activation quantization in our matched-workload comparisons. However, INT4 KV rollout can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). We propose \emph{KV4-RL}, which combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context. Protecting a bounded number of positions reduces sampler mismatch while retaining most of the speedup from INT4. Across 400 iterations of Qwen3-8B-Base GRPO training, KV4-RL achieves $1.80\times$ cumulative rollout speedup and $1.27\times$ cumulative full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout, reaching $1.97\times$ rollout speedup over the final 50 iterations. Under a common BF16 evaluator, its final six-benchmark mean accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.

title: Jevolution: A Framework for Studying Communication and Collective Dynamics in AI Agents
justification: Agent-based predator-prey simulation framework, unrelated.
abstract: Experiments with remote decision-making agents depend on more than the policy: the world may change during inference, the simulator determines which actions are available, and births and immigration alter who can act. We present Jevolution, an instrumented spatial predator-prey framework that makes these dependencies explicit. Its reference implementation separates the evolving world, asynchronous request scheduling, controller adapters, and experiment records. The model combines local observations, energy and resource constraints, predefined signals, and inherited scalar traits. We describe these mechanisms using the ODD protocol and distinguish implemented controls from research questions requiring additional interventions. Free synthetic fixtures exercise scheduling, signaling, and inheritance against the pinned implementation; they validate specified software behavior rather than model intelligence or ecological realism. A completed communication case study illustrates the end-to-end workflow using Jev to control both species. Across 6 complete habitat-seed pairs, the mean signals-on minus signals-off difference in normalized rabbit abundance was -0.0095 (nominal 95% pair-bootstrap interval [-0.0772, 0.0602]). This small study does not resolve the direction of the signal-system effect. The contribution is an inspectable experimental system and its evidence boundaries, not a new policy-learning algorithm or a demonstration of emergent language, adaptive selection, or biological predictive validity.

title: Re-executing Coding-Agent Evaluations: Unchanged Decisions and Unresolved Policy Risk
justification: Re-execution study of coding-agent evaluations, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Touches SWE-bench and Darwin Gödel Machine; eval-robustness interest.
abstract: Executable tests grade large language model (LLM) coding-agent patches for leaderboards, rewards and self-improvement. Two preregistered re-execution studies returned negative results. SWE-bench Pro v1's offline option rejected none of 59 accepted Go patches whose grading configuration changed. Their exploratory, unweighted upper confidence limit is 4.95% under candidate independence, leaving a 3% exposed-patch risk unresolved; the preregistered estimator uses inverse sampling-probability weights. An extension was inconclusive. In a selected stratum, a reconstructed module cache built from the reference solution's dependencies rejected accepted alternatives from four models that passed with their own dependencies. Re-executing 1,929 selected agent-version/task evaluations from the Darwin Gödel Machine's archive preserved best-agent selection and system-variant ranking, with search history and scores of evaluations not rerun fixed. Exploratory host, image and adapted-grader comparisons also preserved them. Seven of 23 disagreements with archived verdicts did not recur on a second host; rebuilt images changed 16 three-run majority verdicts (0.83%) under four-CPU execution. We provide an evidence-to-claim summary, lessons for grader audits and an anonymous replication package. These results concern accepted patches and fixed-history decisions; general policy safety and adaptive-learning robustness require broader evaluations.

title: Evaluating Bias in Chinese Large Language Models across Tasks and Registers: Task Operationalization Effects and Irony Classification Risks
justification: Bias evaluation of Chinese LLMs, unrelated to inference.
abstract: In Chinese content governance, large language models are increasingly used to identify toxic and discriminatory expressions, yet both task operationalization and ironic expression can alter bias measurement readings. We conducted a preregistered multi-task behavioral audit of multiple Chinese large language models. In the content classification experiment, the core panel's classification error rate rose from 10.9% in the formal register to 23.5% in the yinyang (an echoic-irony register) version, a risk difference of +12.7 percentage points. (95% CI [+9.7, +15.7]). Inter-rater agreement was lower in the yinyang register (majority-vote kappa = 0.299), so the increase contains a component of label uncertainty propagation, but the direction of increase was consistent under both adjudicated and majority-vote reference standards. Explicit irony-aware prompts reduced the intervention panel's error rate by 9.6 percentage points. We operationalized the 29 shared proposition anchors into three task forms: social consensus estimation (Form A), high-stakes decision (Form B), and controlled association rating (Form C); independent manipulation checks found that all 58 A-C comparison units received unanimous agreement, whereas the low A-B convergence was confirmed by calibrated majority adjudication (87.8% supporting the minority judgment); on the irony-probe materials, the interactions of B and C relative to A were +0.577 and +1.121, respectively. Thus, when evaluating large language models for Chinese content governance, the effect of task operationalization on bias readings is an empirical question that requires data to answer, and safety evaluation should incorporate the ironic register as a test condition.

title: Diffusion-Based Auctions for Multi-Winner Banner Ads
justification: Diffusion-based ad auctions, unrelated to inference.
hype_justification: Daskalakis co-author lends visibility despite off-topic for this scanner.
abstract: We propose a new framework for banner ad auctions, leveraging diffusion models to allow for multiple bidders to co-win a single banner ad opportunity, and in particular influence the ad shown on the banner depending on the strength of their bids, enabling a far richer outcome space compared to standard banner ad auctions, where there is a single winner who shows their ad. In our framework, the outcomes are images (what ad to show) and each bidder expresses their preferences over outcomes by declaring their value per unit of alignment between the image chosen by the mechanism and a textual description of their desired image. Our proposed mechanism combines the advertisers' bids and textual descriptions into a score that drives the reverse process of a diffusion model. This is used to sample a set of candidate images from which the welfare maximizing one is eventually chosen. Extensive experimentation evaluates our proposed mechanism around the following axes: (1) efficiency improvements of our allocation rule relative to the single-winner allocation rule; (2) monotonicity of our allocation rule; and (3) approximate incentive compatibility when combining our allocation rule with Myerson lemma-based or Clarke rule-based payments. Improvements along all these axes are shown with the number of Monte Carlo samples. Meanwhile, these benefits are attained while preserving the image quality.

title: RES-MR: Risk-Aware Reasoning for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation
justification: Medication recommendation with LLM reasoning, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Clinical LLM application; moderate domain interest.
abstract: Medication recommendations seek to deliver personalized drug combinations based on patients' clinical information, where ensuring transparent decision-making and personalized safety are of paramount importance. However, existing approaches predominantly operate as ``black boxes'', offering limited interpretability and hindering clinician trust. Furthermore, they typically rely on fixed, patient-agnostic safety constraints, neglecting the heterogeneity of risk tolerance across individuals, which poses significant risks to vulnerable populations. To address these gaps, we propose \textbf{RES-MR}, a novel Risk-aware Reasoning framework for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation using LLMs. RES-MR follows a two-stage training paradigm: (1) an explainable clinical reasoning distillation stage to elicit diagnostic capabilities by fine-tuning on synthesized reasoning trajectories, grounded in patient-specific knowledge from graph retrieval; and (2) a risk-aware policy optimization stage to dynamically balance therapeutic efficacy with personalized safety. This stage employs disentangled drug factors to construct patient-specific reference prototypes that capture desired therapeutic drug features and risk features to avoid. These prototypes enable risk boundary calibration and guide the model toward safe recommendations via reward shaping and clipping. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that RES-MR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy, safety, and explainability. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/wangcong2001/RES-MR.

title: EdgeLLM-Nano: Auditing Polar-Guided Key-Cache Compression and Consistency-Anchored Pruning on a 33.6 MB On-Device Language Model
justification: Measurement study auditing KV-cache compression on an on-device model—core inference efficiency.
hype_justification: Rigorous negative-result audit of KV compression; interesting but less flashy, smaller group.
abstract: Deploying language models (LMs) on the edge presents unique memory, latency, and power challenges absent in high-performance computing. KV-cache compression emerges as a promising approach to address these challenges. However, the effectiveness of current KV-cache compression methods has not been thoroughly examined on edge devices. Moreover, we show that existing evaluation methods do not always involve the KV-cache under test. We propose EdgeLLM-Nano, a measurement study of KV-cache compression using a nano-scale decoder-only LM (transformer) testbed that has 8.39M parameters, i.e., 33.6 MB, to enable end-to-end examination of each backend, seed, and power sample. Our results give a negative verdict for a polar-guided key-cache quantizer (round-to-nearest (RTN) control causes an order of magnitude less damage), as well as a consistency-anchored progressive weight pruner (one-shot magnitude-based pruning performs as well as, if not better). We also introduce Long-Context Decode Fidelity (LCDF) evaluation, a token-by-token examination of teacher-forced log-losses using the KV-cache under test. Unlike perplexity that gives the same 5.461 score to all methods, LCDF distinguishes different KV-cache compression backends thanks to its paired statistics across seeds and effect sizes. Our companion Raspberry Pi 5 measurement shows all compression backends we tested to be less energy-efficient per token compared to uncompressed FP16 inference. Except for KIVI that is close to lossless in terms of LCDF, our findings indicate KV-cache compression can be improved. LCDF offers a simple and effective way of shedding light on KV-cache compression methods, whose negative impacts have been overlooked by perplexity.

title: Scale, Drivers, and Limits of Representational Alignment Across Large Language Models
justification: Representational alignment analysis across LLMs, not inference.
abstract: Comparing large language models can reveal shared representational structure and systematic differences between them. However, aggregate similarity measures can obscure how agreement varies across geometric scales and which linguistic properties support it. We introduce two complementary methods to resolve where models agree and what supports that agreement. Standard representational similarity analysis (RSA) summarizes similarity across all stimulus pairs, potentially obscuring differences in alignment between nearby and distant inputs. Neighborhood-Weighted RSA (NW-RSA) addresses this limitation by weighting stimulus pairs according to their proximity in representational space, placing alignment from local neighborhoods to global geometry on a common scale. Counterfactual RSA (CF-RSA) tests which linguistic properties support alignment by comparing intact representations in one model with representations under controlled linguistic perturbations in another. Across diverse language models, we find strong agreement in coarse representational geometry but substantial divergence in local neighborhoods. Alignment is observed both across broadly sampled natural text and within linguistic equivalence classes that preserve particular aspects of meaning or structure. Counterfactual analyses reveal selective sensitivity: changes to logical scope reduce alignment substantially more than the tested changes to hierarchical syntax, event roles, or discourse structure. Alignment also decreases when sentence structure or lexical meaning is disrupted in word lists and jabberwocky sentences, suggesting that the regularities of natural language support stronger convergence. These findings refine claims of representational universality by showing that strong overall similarity need not imply agreement in how models represent finer linguistic distinctions.

title: TurboProm: Low Cost and High Performance Metrics Observability at Scale
justification: Prometheus metrics observability acceleration—general systems, not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Open-source systems tool, niche observability audience.
abstract: Many large enterprise and cloud deployments rely on metrics observability solutions (e.g., Prometheus) to monitor key performance indicators of system health (e.g., CPU, memory, network, app-level statistics). Monitoring and analyzing these metrics presents a significant challenge in terms of cost-latency tradeoffs at scale. Ideally, system operators would like immediately deployable and backwards compatible solutions to improve the cost-latency tradeoffs without significant impact on the fidelity of their observability applications. Unfortunately, existing solutions including state-of-art timeseries databases and custom approximate querying solutions fail on one or more aspects. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of TurboProm, a backwards-compatible drop-in accelerator for metrics observability deployments. TurboProm recasts metrics analytics tasks using a semantic-preserving summary view rather than classical query-centric view. Instead of estimating query results on raw timeseries metrics data, TurboProm uses semantic-preserving summaries that enable high-fidelity analytics with significant cost-latency improvements. We present a practical implementation of TurboProm that can be retrofitted to any existing observability deployment. We evaluate TurboProm on diverse real and synthetic workloads against state-of-art solutions and show that it can provide significant reduction in query latency and cost. TurboProm is open-source at https://github.com/ProjectASAP/ASAPQuery.

title: A Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM) for Physically-Interpretable Rainfall-Evapotranspiration-Runoff Simulation Across Diverse Hydroclimatic Regimes
justification: Hydrology rainfall-runoff model, unrelated.
abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have improved rainfall-runoff prediction, yet most data-driven models remain difficult to interpret and do not explicitly enforce physical conservation laws. We present the Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM), a mass-conserving architecture based on the Mass-Conserving Perceptron (MCP). GCHM uses five storage states representing canopy interception, snow, soil moisture, groundwater, and streamflow generation. Constrained gates govern precipitation partitioning, evapotranspiration, infiltration, seepage, runoff, and baseflow while learning context-dependent process relationships. We evaluate GCHM across 50 CAMELS catchments spanning snowmelt-dominated, recent-rainfall, historical-rainfall, and arid regimes, using NOAA AORC meteorological forcing and remotely sensed vegetation and land-surface data. Performance is assessed using the Jawad-Kling-Gupta Efficiency (JKGE) metric, which accounts for stationary and non-stationary hydrologic behavior. We compare the full architecture with ablated variants and recurrent neural network benchmarks. GCHM reproduces streamflow dynamics across diverse hydroclimatic regimes, including arid catchments, while maintaining interpretable states and fluxes. Ablation experiments show that simplified architectures may perform adequately under wet conditions but struggle to represent flow persistence and recession during dry periods, when groundwater storage sustains low flows. Learned gates recover hydrologically plausible relationships governing snowmelt, runoff, seepage, and evapotranspiration. GCHM combines competitive predictive performance with mass conservation and interpretability, providing a foundation for hydrologic modeling and counterfactual analysis.

title: Rethinking Activation Functions: Reducing Bias Can Improve Learning
justification: Activation-function bias and learning dynamics—training-side, not inference.
hype_justification: Broadly applicable architecture insight could get moderate attention.
abstract: Many widely used activation functions, including ReLU, GELU, Swish, and Sigmoid, produce predominantly positive outputs, resulting in a nonzero post-activation mean that we term activation bias. Despite its ubiquity, the effect of activation bias on learning dynamics remains poorly understood. Using controlled models, we show that activation bias accelerates initial loss reduction but is accompanied by overshooting, non-smooth trajectories, and a steeper loss landscape. This early advantage also coincides with the model's use of task-relevant information encoded in the activation bias component. In contrast, reducing activation bias slows initial learning but ultimately yields a lower final loss. Experiments on larger vision and language models exhibit a similar pattern: smaller activation bias is associated with better late-stage performance. Thus, this seemingly minor property can substantially redirect learning and warrants explicit consideration in future activation function design.

title: Compositional Concepts Erasing: Disentangling Object-Style via Domain Manifold Unlearning
justification: Diffusion concept unlearning, unrelated to inference.
hype_justification: Unlearning/safety is topical but this is specialized.
abstract: Diffusion models pose significant risks regarding the generation of illicit content and copyright violations. This has catalyzed the development of machine unlearning to erase harmful concepts or copyrighted styles from a model's generative repertoire without compromising its general performance. However, previous unlearning approaches on diffusion models have largely focused on either object-level or style-level removal and failed to address the challenge of object-style combination unlearning. At the same time, multiple unlearning requests often lead to catastrophic forgetting. To address these challenges, we propose Domain Manifold Unlearning (DMU), which uses an EMA-updated feature proxy extracted from intermediate diffusion features to represent the retained target-object direction. As a lightweight estimating representation of an object, DMU enables selective unlearning of domain-specific components in a specific object while preserving other semantic representations, thereby significantly enhancing robustness in multiple combination unlearning scenarios. Extensive experiments show that DMU significantly mitigates catastrophic forgetting, outperforming state-of-the-art methods of batch unlearning and sequential unlearning.

title: Query-Adaptive Neuron Steering for LLMs
justification: Query-adaptive neuron steering elicits capabilities at inference time but is an intervention method, not a serving/system optimization.
hype_justification: Activation steering is trendy; frozen-model query-adaptive angle is novel.
abstract: Effectively eliciting the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) at inference time remains an important challenge. Existing studies address this challenge through context engineering, which shapes user queries, or fixed steering, which directly intervenes in model computation. However, predefined contexts and fixed intervention strategies may not adequately accommodate the diverse knowledge and reasoning requirements of individual queries. This raises a natural question: Can internal steering in LLMs be made query-adaptive? In this work, we investigate whether query-induced internal activations can guide adaptive steering in LLMs. Our pilot studies reveal subject- and layer-dependent neuron activation patterns and show that amplifying subject-relevant neurons can improve model performance. Based on these findings, we propose Q-NeuS, a query-adaptive neuron steering framework that dynamically determines which neurons to modulate and by how much for each input. Specifically, Q-NeuS constructs a compact subject-guided candidate neuron space and employs a lightweight Query-Adaptive Gate to generate neuron-wise modulation coefficients. To learn effective intervention strategies, we introduce Neu-GRPO, which adapts group-relative optimization to train the Query-Adaptive Gate using the relative performance of multiple neuron intervention configurations. The base LLM remains frozen throughout training and inference, and no task or subject labels are required at inference time. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that Q-NeuS consistently improves model performance and exhibits broad applicability across model scales and strong cross-benchmark transferability.

title: Energy Ring: Stabilizing Feature Energy for Reliable Test-Time Discovery
justification: Test-time discovery energy method, unrelated to inference serving.
abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones while the model is already deployed, operating directly on a continual unlabeled test-time stream. Existing TTD methods are overly conservative, making known and unknown features collapse together and difficult to separate during test-time adaptation. In this paper, we revisit TTD from an energy perspective and find that the natural energy gap between known and unknown classes is unstable and easily collapses. We therefore propose Energy Ring to stabilize this gap by anchoring the two types of classes on separate energy rings. A lightweight adapter enlarges the norm-based gap while preserving known-class directions, and a perturbation consistency module forms compact clusters for unknown classes. During testing, energy-guided confidence weighting improves prediction, and a stability-based rectification mechanism corrects unreliable updates. Experimental results show that Energy Ring significantly improves TTD performance against existing TTD methods.

title: Who to Trust in Multi-Robot Systems: Joint Robot and Object Hypothesis Trust Inference via Neural-Symbolic Cross-Validation
justification: Multi-robot trust inference, unrelated.
abstract: Multi-robot systems (MRS) offer significant advantages over single-robot platforms by enabling information sharing and coordination for different tasks in complex environments. However, reliable cooperation critically depends on inferring trust over both information sources and their reported hypotheses, particularly under partial observability and potential adversarial interference. Existing approaches frequently depend on pre-established trust relationships or side-channel information, which may not be available or reliable in realistic MRS deployments. This work introduces NeST-Bayes, a neural-symbolic framework that jointly infers robot and hypothesis trust using only inter-robot observation consistency, without requiring preassigned robot trust, reputation information, or side-channel identity signals. NeST-Bayes infers instantaneous trust evidence scores for robots and object hypotheses by reasoning over ego-centric relational graphs constructed from cross-robot observation consistency. These evidence scores are accumulated over time through Bayesian updates of Beta-distributed trust beliefs to maintain temporally consistent trust estimates. Extensive evaluations show that NeST-Bayes achieves the highest mean object precision and robot recall across all benchmark settings, and the highest robot precision and object recall in most settings, compared to trust-based methods. Under aggressive optimized attacks, it achieves 98.8\% robot precision with 93.8\% recall and 98.3\% object precision with 95.4\% recall. In an occlusion-rich Webots warehouse, it maintains 92.5\% robot precision with 92.0\% recall and 97.3\% object precision with 85.0\% recall. These results demonstrate joint improvements in the reliability and coverage of retained information.

title: LongHisDoc: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chinese Long Historical Document Understanding
justification: Chinese historical document understanding benchmark, not inference.
abstract: Chinese historical documents are invaluable cultural treasures, but their complexity poses significant comprehension challenges for non-specialists. Despite the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) in modern document tasks, their capabilities in Long (full-book) Historical Document understanding remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce LongHisDoc, the first benchmark tailored for long historical document understanding. LongHisDoc comprises 1,012 expert-annotated QA pairs derived from 101 PDF documents, with an average of 85.1 pages and 42,776.4 tokens per document. It spans 10 categories and features four QA types: single-page, cross-page, multi-hop, and unanswerable. Answering these questions requires integrating multimodal evidence from text, layout, and visual elements. Our evaluation reveals that the top-performing LVLM and LLM achieve only 62.9% and 69.9% accuracy, respectively, highlighting a substantial performance gap. Furthermore, we assess various modal retrievers and the end-to-end RAG performance to provide references for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. We believe that LongHisDoc serves as a comprehensive benchmark to catalyze future research in full-book historical document understanding. The benchmark and evaluation code are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/qweq12433454/LongHisDoc and https://github.com/SCUT-DLVCLab/LongHisDoc.

title: GMM: Generalized OS Memory Management for Programmable XPUs
justification: Generalized OS memory management for XPUs; reports inference-serving switch latency and GPU memory savings relevant to serving infrastructure.
hype_justification: Nvidia/Huawei driver-level systems work with strong numbers; appeals to systems audience.
abstract: Since the AI boom, the fast evolving programmable XPU devices utilize high-bandwidth local memory to accelerate domain-specific tasks offloaded from the host CPU, resulting in a proliferation of XPU memory management systems implemented in proprietary drivers. However, existing OS core memory management (MM) continues to lack a high-level software abstraction, excluding the XPUs from leveraging OS advanced memory features. The XPU manufacturers have to reimplement independent XPU MM drivers, exacerbating the fragmented XPU software ecosystem. This paper presents GMM, generalized memory management that provides unified MM subsystems for XPUs. By adding an explicit logical mapping abstraction, GMM 1) provides universal NUMA-aware memory API for XPUs; 2) allows ease of XPU MM delegation; 3) enables sharing of advanced XPU memory features. Lightweight XPU MM drivers are implemented for two representative XPU manufacturers, Nvidia and Huawei. Both GMM-based drivers obtain competitive performance compared with their vendor-supplied drivers. GMM also obtains up to 41% higher fault-driven page migration throughput. Two real-world industrial case studies are exercised, where GMM reduces XPU memory utilization by 10% with up to 22.6x faster inference serving switch latency.

title: GG-Nav: Goal-oriented Grounding Chain-of-Thought Elicits Reasoning in Navigation Foundation Models
justification: Goal-oriented navigation CoT, unrelated to inference.
hype_justification: Embodied navigation with real-robot demo; moderate interest.
abstract: Emerging strong Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have advanced navigation foundation models. However, these models still have unsatisfactory performance on goal-oriented navigation settings. In this paper, we first conduct a motivating study revealing that the key issue lies in the insufficient utilization of streaming observations and imprecise target localization. To tackle these challenges, we propose GG-Nav, a simple yet effective navigation framework that learns a structured chain-of-thought (CoT) mechanism via supervised fine-tuning to explicitly localize goal-relevant instances, accumulate grounding evidence, and support more reliable decision-making.
