LLMs implement conditional distributions over outputs, not fixed functions. Collapsing these distributions to a single canonical completion may appear reassuring, but it systematically conceals properties central to artificial cognition. We instead advocate Stochastic CHAOS, treating distributional variability as a signal to be measured and controlled. Empirically, we show that deterministic inference is systematically misleading. Single-sample deterministic evaluation underestimates both capability and fragility, masking failure probability under paraphrases and noise. Phase-like transitions associated with emergent abilities disappear under greedy decoding. Multi-path reasoning degrades when forced onto deterministic backbones, reducing accuracy and diagnostic insight. Finally, deterministic evaluation underestimates safety risk by hiding rare but dangerous behaviors that appear only under multi-sample evaluation.

title: Representational Similarity Alignment of Figurative Language in Humans and Large Language Models
justification: Representational similarity of figurative language in humans vs LLMs, cognition study.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce judgments similar to those of humans, but their interpretation of figurative language remains unclear. We compared human participants and four instruction-tuned LLMs (GPT-4, Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3.2, and Mistral-7B) on their ratings of 240 dialogue-based sentences spanning six linguistic traits: conventionality, sarcasm, funny, emotion, idiomacy, and Gen Z slang. While humans and LLMs were strongly aligned at the surface level, differences emerged in representational similarity patterns, particularly in idiomacy and Gen Z slang. GPT-4 showed the closest alignment to humans, though all models differed at the representational level, suggesting that similar outputs may arise from different underlying language representations. We also examined the relationship between model scale and representational similarity using the Gemma model series (Gemma-2-9B-IT, Gemma-3-27B-IT, and Gemma-4-31B-IT), and found that representational similarity patterns were largely unaffected by model size.

title: Less is More: Label-Guided Efficient Summarization of Procedural and Instructional Videos
justification: Training-free frame-efficient video summarization; selective inference design but vision-language application.
abstract: Video summarization transforms long videos into concise representations that are easier to document and analyze, especially in high-stakes domains such as surgical training. However, long-form videos often require dense frame processing or supervised training pipelines, which can be computationally expensive and may still miss important procedural content. We present PRISM: Procedural Representation via Integrated Semantic and Multimodal Analysis, a zero-shot and training-free framework for frame-efficient procedural video summarization. PRISM selects fewer than 5% of video frames while retaining over 84% semantic content and improving over baselines by up to 7.5%. Rather than exhaustively processing frames, PRISM uses lightweight visual filtering and dynamically generated procedural labels as semantic anchors to select meaningful frame-label groups. This selective inference design preserves key actions, transitions, and contextual details while reducing the number of visual inputs passed to downstream vision-language captioning stages. We evaluate PRISM on YouCook2 and ActivityNet Captions, with additional studies on keyframe selection benchmarks and surgical video datasets. Across procedural and domain-specific video tasks, PRISM achieves strong semantic alignment and accuracy, suggesting that efficient multimodal video understanding can be achieved by grounding generation in dynamically generated semantic anchors.

title: VERGE: Formal Refinement and Guidance Engine for Verifiable LLM Reasoning
justification: Neurosymbolic SMT-guided verifiable reasoning, reasoning method.
abstract: Despite the syntactic fluency of Large Language Models (LLMs), ensuring their logical correctness in high-stakes domains remains a fundamental challenge. We present a neurosymbolic framework that combines LLMs with SMT solvers to produce verification-guided answers through iterative refinement. Our approach decomposes LLM outputs into atomic claims, autoformalizes them into first-order logic, and verifies their logical consistency using automated theorem proving. We introduce three key innovations: (1) multi-model consensus via formal semantic equivalence checking to ensure logic-level alignment between candidates, eliminating the syntactic bias of surface-form metrics, (2) semantic routing that directs different claim types to appropriate verification strategies: symbolic solvers for logical claims and LLM ensembles for commonsense reasoning, and (3) precise logical error localization via Minimal Correction Subsets (MCS), which pinpoint the exact subset of claims to revise, transforming binary failure signals into actionable feedback. Our framework classifies claims by their logical status and aggregates multiple verification signals into a unified score with variance-based penalty. The system iteratively refines answers using structured feedback until acceptance criteria are met or convergence is achieved. This hybrid approach delivers formal guarantees where possible and consensus verification elsewhere, advancing trustworthy AI. With the GPT-OSS-120B model, VERGE demonstrates an average performance uplift of 18.7% at convergence across a set of reasoning benchmarks compared to single-pass approaches.

title: Towards Optimality in Active Preference Learning
justification: Active preference learning for alignment data, theory.
abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) depends on high-quality datasets of human preference labels, which are costly to collect. Although active learning has been studied to improve sample efficiency relative to passive collection, many existing approaches adopt classical experimental design criteria such as G- or D-optimality. These objectives are not tailored to the structure of preference learning, leaving open the design of problem-specific algorithms. In this work, we identify a simple intuition specific to preference learning that calls into question the suitability of these existing design objectives. Motivated by this insight, we propose two active learning algorithms. The first provides the first instance-dependent label complexity guarantee for this setting, and the second is a simple, practical greedy method. We show the optimality of our instance-dependent term up to a constant depending on the logit bound, compared with a lower-bound characteristic. We evaluate our algorithms on real-world preference datasets and synthetic data observing improved sample efficiency compared to existing methods.

title: Risky-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Safety Risks in Real-World Life-Assist Deployments
justification: Agentic safety benchmark for life-assist deployments, evaluation.
hype_justification: Agent safety benchmark topical but eval-focused.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that operate in real-world environments, introducing safety risks beyond linguistic harm through tool use, external transactions, and multi-step decision making. Existing agent safety evaluations construct risk-oriented tasks that lack a hierarchically organized taxonomy of attack surfaces, rely on predefined harm categories rather than deployment-grounded safety rubrics, and evaluate agent behavior in isolation rather than during realistic, long-horizon task execution. To address these limitations, we propose Risky-Bench, a deployment-grounded framework for systematic agent safety evaluation in life-assist settings. Risky-Bench derives context-aware safety rubrics from domain-agnostic safety principles and systematically probes safety risks across hierarchically organized attack surfaces through realistic task execution under varying threat assumptions. Applied to life-assist scenarios covering food delivery, in-store assistance, and online travel booking, Risky-Bench evaluates seven state-of-the-art agents across 750 tasks, revealing attack success rates ranging from 25% to 60% and exposing systematic failure patterns including threat-model-specific vulnerabilities, attack-surface-dependent risk concentration, and model-dependent effects of explicit reasoning. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/SophieZheng998/Risky-Bench.

title: DRMOT: A Dataset and Framework for RGBD Referring Multi-Object Tracking
justification: RGBD referring multi-object tracking dataset; unrelated to LLM inference.
hype_justification: Niche tracking dataset, limited broad attention.
abstract: Referring Multi-Object Tracking (RMOT) aims to track specific targets based on language descriptions, playing a vital role in interactive AI systems such as robotics and autonomous driving. However, existing RMOT methods rely exclusively on 2D RGB observations. Since similar 2D projections can correspond to different 3D configurations, the available observations may not uniquely determine the referred targets. This creates a fundamental mismatch between the task requirements and the available input. To advance research on the DRMOT task, we construct DRSet, a dataset tailored for the DRMOT task. DRSet comprises 2,076 referring expressions over 186 RGB-D source sequences. It features synchronized RGB images and depth maps paired with language descriptions, including explicit depth-dependent descriptions, to systematically evaluate spatial-semantic detection and tracking capabilities. Furthermore, we propose DRTrack, an MLLM-guided depth-referring tracking framework. DRTrack leverages a Geometric-Aware GRPO fine-tuned Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) to achieve precise spatial-semantic detection from joint L+RGB+D inputs, while incorporating explicit depth cues to enforce robust trajectory association. Extensive experiments on the DRSet dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework. Our dataset and code will be available at https://github.com/chen-si-jia/DRMOT.

title: PACC: Protocol-Aware Cross-Layer Compression for Compact Network Traffic Representation
justification: Network traffic classification compression; not LLM inference.
abstract: Network traffic classification underpins network security and management but faces growing challenges from pervasive encryption and evolving protocols. Existing representations involve clear trade-offs: hand-crafted flow statistics are efficient but lossy, raw-bit encodings can be accurate but costly, and pre-trained embeddings support transfer but often flatten the protocol stack and entangle cross-layer signals. We observe substantial redundancy both across and within network layers, which existing paradigms do not explicitly address, wasting capacity and encouraging shortcut learning that degrades generalization. To address this, we propose PACC, a redundancy-aware cross-layer representation framework. PACC models protocol layers as multiview inputs and learns faithful, compact projections factorized into shared (cross-layer) and private (layer-specific) components. It incorporates an information-preserving sparse segment representation to reduce structural repetition and supervised intra-layer filtering to suppress task-irrelevant semantic redundancy. A behavior-guided shared/private decomposition aligns cross-layer consensus while retaining layer-specific information, supported by information-theoretic analysis. Across encrypted application classification, IoT device identification, benign/malicious traffic classification, and Tor traffic detection, PACC achieves the best overall performance. On encrypted traffic, it achieves an F1 score of 0.9685, substantially outperforming existing baselines while using approximately 15x fewer computes and less GPU memory than the latest pre-trained traffic model.

title: Learning Ordinal Probabilistic Reward from Preferences
justification: Reward modeling for LLM alignment, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Reward models are trending but this is incremental.
abstract: Reward models are crucial for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values and intentions. Existing approaches follow either Generative (GRMs) or Discriminative (DRMs) paradigms, yet both suffer from limitations: GRMs typically demand costly point-wise supervision, while DRMs produce uncalibrated relative scores that lack probabilistic interpretation. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel reward modeling paradigm: Probabilistic Reward Model (PRM). Instead of modeling reward as a deterministic scalar, our approach treats it as a random variable, learning a full probability distribution for the quality of each response. To make this paradigm practical, we present its closed-form, discrete realization: the Ordinal Probabilistic Reward Model (OPRM), which discretizes the quality score into a finite set of ordinal ratings. Building on OPRM, we propose a data-efficient training strategy called Region Flooding Tuning (RgFT). It enables rewards to better reflect absolute text quality by incorporating quality-level annotations, which guide the model to concentrate the probability mass within corresponding rating sub-regions. Experiments on various reward model benchmarks show that our method improves accuracy by $\textbf{2.9%}\sim\textbf{7.4%}$ compared to prior reward models, demonstrating strong performance and data efficiency. Analysis of the score distribution provides evidence that our method captures not only relative rankings but also absolute quality.

title: Circumventing the CAP Theorem with Open Æthernet
justification: Networking/CAP theorem hardware fabric; unrelated.
abstract: The CAP theorem is routinely treated as a systems law: under network partition, a replicated service must sacrifice either consistency or availability. The theorem is correct within its standard asynchronous network model, but operational practice depends on where partition-like phenomena become observable and on how lower layers discard or preserve semantic information about message fate. This paper argues that Open Æthernet (OAE) shifts the engineering regime in which CAP tradeoffs become application-visible by (i) replacing fire-and-forget link semantics with bounded-time bilateral reconciliation of endpoint state -- the property we call bisynchrony -- and (ii) avoiding Clos funnel points via an octavalent mesh in which each node can act as the root of a locally repaired spanning tree. The result is not the elimination of hard graph cuts, but a drastic reduction in the frequency and duration of application-visible "soft partitions" by detecting and healing dominant fabric faults within hundreds of nanoseconds, under the link-fault model and repair rule stated in the paper. We connect this view to Brewer's original CAP framing, the formalization by Gilbert and Lynch, the CAL theorem of Lee et al., which replaces binary partition tolerance with a quantitative measure of apparent latency, and Abadi's PACELC extension.

title: A Counterfactual Graph Approach to Oppositional Narrative Analysis
justification: Counterfactual graph for narrative analysis; unrelated.
abstract: Distinguishing legitimate critical speech from coordinated conspiracy narratives is a pressing challenge for the integrity of the online information ecosystem, yet prevailing approaches rely on labeled entity roles and rigid predefined schemas that fail to capture the diffuse and context-dependent nature of participation in such narratives. We propose a modular framework that extracts an entity-interaction graph directly from narratives and reasons over it for classification, without depending on annotated node-level labels. Our pipeline enumerates candidate entity spans from a domain-adapted BERT encoder and learns a bipartite graph structure, which is then classified with a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer. To make predictions interpretable, we cast the graph as a hypergraph and apply a counterfactual distillation procedure that estimates the Individual Treatment Effect of each node, pruning extraneous entities to recover a minimal predictive subgraph. On the standard PAN Oppositional Narratives benchmark, our model achieves a macro F1-score of 0.93 and an MCC of 0.84, reaching state-of-the-art performance with roughly one-third of the parameters of the next best system, while pruning the graphs by 75.2% on average without altering predictions. Our results demonstrate that graph-based representations coupled with counterfactual inference offer both strong predictive accuracy and transparency into the entities driving conspiratorial discourse.

title: IMAGAgent: Orchestrating Multi-Turn Image Editing via Constraint-Aware Planning and Reflection
justification: Multi-turn image editing agent; not inference systems.
hype_justification: Image editing agents are popular but crowded space.
abstract: Existing multi-turn image editing paradigms are often confined to isolated single-step execution. Due to a lack of context-awareness and closed-loop feedback mechanisms, they are prone to error accumulation and semantic drift during multi-turn interactions, ultimately resulting in severe structural distortion of the generated images. To address this, we propose IMAGAgent, a multi-turn image editing agent framework based on a ``plan--execute--reflect'' closed-loop mechanism that achieves deep synergy among instruction parsing, tool scheduling, and adaptive correction within a unified pipeline. Specifically, we first present a constraint-aware planning module that leverages a vision-language model (VLM) to precisely decompose complex natural language instructions into a series of executable sub-tasks, governed by target singularity, semantic atomicity, and visual perceptibility. Then, the tool-chain orchestration module dynamically constructs execution paths based on the current image, the current sub-task, and the historical context, enabling adaptive scheduling and collaborative operation among heterogeneous operation models covering image retrieval, segmentation, detection, and editing. Finally, we devise a multi-expert collaborative reflection mechanism in which a central large language model (LLM) synthesizes evaluations from multiple vision-language models into holistic feedback, triggering fine-grained self-correction and recording feedback outcomes to optimize future decisions. Extensive experiments on our constructed MTEditBench and the MagicBrush dataset demonstrate that IMAGAgent achieves performance significantly superior to existing methods in terms of instruction consistency, editing precision, and overall quality. The code is available at https://github.com/hackermmzz/IMAGAgent.

title: The causal relation between off-street parking and electric vehicle adoption in Scotland
justification: EV adoption causal study; entirely unrelated.
hype_justification: Policy/social science, no ML systems audience.
abstract: The transition to electric mobility hinges on maximising aggregate adoption while also facilitating equitable access. This study examines whether the 'charging divide' between households with and without off-street parking reflects a genuine infrastructure constraint or a by-product of socio-economic disparity. Moving beyond conventional predictive models, we apply a probabilistic causal framework to a nationally representative dataset of Scottish households, enabling estimation of policy interventions while explicitly neutralising the confounding effect of other causal factors. The results reveal a structural hierarchy in the EV adoption process. Private off-street parking functions as a conversion catalyst: enabling access to home-charging increases the probability of EV ownership from 3.3% to 5.6% (a 70% relative, 2.3 percentage point absolute increase). However, this effect primarily accelerates households already economically positioned to purchase an EV rather than recruiting new entrants. By contrast, household income operates as the fundamental affordability ceiling. A causal contrast between lower- and higher-income strata, shows a reduction in market non-participation by 23.1 percentage points, identifying financial capacity as the principal gatekeeper to entering the EV transition funnel. Crucially, the analysis demonstrates that standard observational models overstate the isolated effect of off-street parking infrastructure. The apparent effect emerges from selection bias: higher-income households are disproportionately likely to possess both private parking and the means to purchase EVs. These findings support a dual-track policy strategy: lowering the affordability ceiling for non-participants through financial instruments, while addressing EV home-charging access for the 'latent intent' cohort in high-density urban contexts.

title: Conditioned in Training, Dispensable at Inference: Typological Conditioning for Multilingual Speech Translation
justification: Multilingual speech translation conditioning; 'inference' in title is incidental, about training signal.
abstract: Multilingual speech translation frontends built on speech large language models typically condition on language identity, as a learned embedding or a prompted language name. Such a signal, however, is learned separately for each language and transfers nothing between typologically related languages. In this paper, we present TypoCast, a frontend that conditions on the typological profile of the source language rather than on its label alone. A typology-informed hierarchical language encoding represents each language by its morphological type, constituent order and family, so that supervision is shared among related languages. A dual-route mixture-of-experts adapter routes inputs through a shared typological route together with a per-language residual, and a typology-aware prompt conveys the same profile to the decoder. Extensive experiments on CVSS-C demonstrate that TypoCast surpasses state-of-the-art speech-to-speech translation systems on French, German and Spanish to English, averaged over the three directions, and outperforms the identity-conditioned S2ST-Omni on every language of a seven-language inventory, with only 228M trainable parameters. Ablation studies further reveal that the conditioning signal acts during training and is dispensable at inference: a model trained without it is consistently worse, whereas removing it from a trained model changes BLEU by less than 0.2, and expert usage is consistent with the signal shaping how adapter capacity is divided among languages.

title: Business World Model
justification: Business world model concept paper; not inference.
abstract: World model has emerged as a powerful paradigm in artificial intelligence, enabling agents to represent their environments, predict future states, and evaluate possible actions before acting. However, existing world models have largely been developed for visual or physical domains such as computer vision, robotics, gaming, and autonomous driving, which are governed by relatively stable dynamics. These formulations are not directly applicable to business practice, where the relevant environment is semantic, organizational, and market-driven, and outcomes depend on context-sensitive factors such as customer behavior, pricing, competition, and regulation. This paper introduces the concept and architecture of a Business World Model (BWM), a world model specialized for business and organizational environments. We propose a business-semantics-centric formulation in which states, dynamics, and feasible actions are linked to business entities, their attributes, and their relationships. Within this framework, intelligent agents can simulate alternative action sequences, estimate their effects on future business outcomes, and evaluate trade-offs under uncertainty and business constraints. We present a reference design and open-source implementation in which LLM agents interpret natural-language business goals and explain results, while a deterministic, metadata-driven simulation engine integrating machine learning models, business rules, and action spaces performs all calculations. A churn case study of a media subscription business demonstrates that the system recommends options meeting the churn-reduction target within the revenue constraint. This work establishes a conceptual foundation for autonomous business systems capable of moving from instruction-based execution toward goal-driven planning, optimization, and execution.

title: ManifoldFlow: Spectrum-Learnable Stiefel Optimization via SPD Relaxation
justification: Stiefel/SPD optimization for neural nets; training geometry, not inference.
abstract: Orthogonal and Stiefel constraints help control weight geometry, improve conditioning, and stabilize signal propagation in neural networks. However, standard Stiefel optimization fixes the represented singular values at one, preventing the model from learning direction-dependent amplification or attenuation. We introduce ManifoldFlow, a spectrum-learnable extension of Stiefel optimization that separates an orthonormal factor from a bounded symmetric positive-definite (SPD) spectral factor. The SPD factor equals the Gram matrix of the realized weight, providing exact spectral interpretability and recovering standard Stiefel optimization when set to the identity. ManifoldFlow uses the gradient component rejected by the Stiefel constraint to guide spectral adaptation. By aligning and accumulating this information over time, the method jointly updates the orthonormal basis and the bounded spectrum. We establish the geometry of the rejected gradient, characterize optimization on the Stiefel-SPD product space, and analyze how the learned spectrum affects conditioning, signal propagation, and spectral complexity. Across diverse tasks, ManifoldFlow consistently outperforms matched fixed-spectrum Stiefel baselines, with particularly strong gains in recurrent language modeling.

title: HALLMARK: How to Diagnose LLM Citation Verifiers and When to Deploy Them
justification: Citation hallucination verifier benchmark; not inference systems.
hype_justification: Hallucinated citations is a hot, relatable topic that may draw attention.
abstract: GPTZero found 53 NeurIPS 2025 accepted papers with hallucinated citations, and venues now screen submissions with automated reference checkers. Rule- and Large Language Model (LLM)-based verifiers are emerging, but many are released without a shared evaluation and each flags a different kind of error, so it is unclear which to trust or when to deploy them. We address this with HALLMARK (Hallucination benchmark): 2,526 BibTeX entries spanning 14 hallucination types, with per-type and diagnostic sub-test labels and further temporal, cross-domain, and real-world evaluation splits. We evaluate zero-shot and tool-augmented LLMs, a DOI-lookup baseline, and our own co-designed rule-based verifier, bibtex-updater. Verifiers can miss hallucinations and wrongly flag correct papers, so every flag still needs human review. The false positive rate (FPR) determines the review effort and thus limits deployment. The tested models exhibit an order-of-magnitude spread in FPR; agentic lookups buy recall but inflate FPR, and neither smaller models nor prompt optimization reach the frontier's operating point. A two-stage cascade with bibtex-updater avoids that inflation, providing an upper bound, given the co-design. These rankings, however, depend on what counts as a hallucination: re-scoring the types that describe a real work cited inaccurately changes which verifier ranks first, and venues have not agreed on a definition. We call for a community definition and release per-type labels and a re-scoring protocol so that any agreed definition can be scored against every verifier.

title: Diffusion ReRoll: Revisable Denoising for Robotic Sequential Prediction
justification: Diffusion for robotic sequence prediction; unrelated to LLM inference.
abstract: We propose Diffusion ReRoll, a diffusion-based framework for robotic sequential prediction that enables revisable denoising over horizons. Existing diffusion-based sequence predictors typically perform a single monotonic denoising process. In contrast, Diffusion ReRoll selectively re-noises regions that reach a predefined noise threshold while the remaining regions continue denoising, so the re-noised regions can be refined again using context from the rest of the horizon. This structured re-noising enables iterative cross-horizon revision, allowing earlier and later segments to revise one another, while maintaining local consistency. We evaluate Diffusion ReRoll against full-sequence diffusion and causal denoising based on Diffusion Forcing across long-horizon planning, policy learning, unified video-action modeling, and real-world navigation. On OGBench PointMaze and AntMaze, Diffusion ReRoll achieves relative gains in average success rate of 21% over Diffusion Forcing in matched guidance-based planning and 23% over Diffuser in goal-inpainting. In diffusion-policy-style action prediction, Diffusion ReRoll improves average success by 56.5% relative to Diffusion Policy across different prediction horizons and history lengths on LIBERO-10 under the official reset protocol. In unified video-action prediction, Diffusion ReRoll improves policy and inverse dynamics performance, especially under out-of-distribution evaluation, and achieves the best action-video consistency. Real-world navigation further demonstrates improved success under visual distribution shifts with onboard inference. These results show that structured re-noising enables cross-horizon revision and improves performance across robotic sequential prediction tasks.

title: COSI-Lab: Conference Living Lab for Modeling Multi-Perspective Multimodal Social Intention
justification: Social intention multimodal dataset; unrelated.
abstract: COSI-Lab presents a multimodal multi-sensor dataset of a real interdisciplinary scientific workshop with 32 academics at an international conference. It captures ecologically valid social interactions in a weakly scripted setting consisting of two 30-minute mingling sessions with real professional and social consequences. We argue that intelligent systems could better handle subjective perceptions by modeling their multiplicity not as label noise but as an explainable perspective-driven reasoning process. We focus on the Apparent Intent Inference (AII) problem as determined by ex-situ observers and conceptualize intentions to be independent of the future. We contribute a novel annotation process for AII that accounts for a perceiver's own interpretative tendencies, quantitative and qualitative analyses of intent narratives with respect to diversity, plausibility and grounding, benchmark tasks for AII and relevant contextual factors, speech quality audio for all participants as well as privacy-preserving multi-modal environmental and wearable sensor data, enabling lexical and nonverbal behavior analysis; and the coupling of self-reported participant goals (30 minute to 3 hour) with annotated AII (seconds).

title: QASP: Query-Adaptive Robust Vector Search Policy
justification: Query-adaptive vector search; relevant to retrieval serving but not LLM inference core.
hype_justification: Vector search has a database audience; Warfield coauthor adds some draw.
abstract: A fundamental challenge of vector search is achieving consistently high recall while minimizing computational costs. Fixed search parameters cause significant performance variance across queries, and conventional evaluation on average recall masks these per-query disparities. We introduce QASP (Query-Adaptive robust vector Search Policy), which predicts the complete recall progression curve per query via a single upfront supervised regression, from which a search policy is derived for any recall target; this avoids iterative model invocations during search or separate predictors per target. By predicting normalized recall values with scale-invariant features and pre-search inference, QASP generalizes across recall targets, index configurations, and datasets. Its fine-grained progress predictions further enable a lightweight reactive complement that adjusts search depth based on predicted-versus-observed deviations without additional inference. We prove that QASP requires a finite training sample independent of dataset size and dimensionality, that its loss exceeds the irreducible lower bound of any fixed policy by a vanishing margin, and that its data access savings over fixed probing grow exponentially in intrinsic dimensionality. Experimentally, QASP achieves significantly lower recall variance and deviation from target, higher query satisfaction rate, and scales to large data and hierarchical indices without retraining, achieving 99% recall with 80% less data access.

title: Lost in Context Compaction: When LLM Systems Drop Side Constraints
justification: Context compaction in LLM agent systems; tangential to serving/context management.
hype_justification: Context compaction and agent safety is a hot practical topic with IBM authors.
abstract: When the context window is under pressure, LLM systems compact prior context to continue ongoing tasks. We study Side Constraints (SCs), user-issued instructions such as "do not delete any emails until I confirm," that constrain an LLM's behavior across subsequent turns but can be silently dropped during compaction. In an inbox experiment, an agent deleted emails without approval in 30/100 sessions after compaction, compared with none before compaction. To systematically evaluate SC preservation, we introduce CONPACT, an evaluation suite measuring semantic retention and downstream compliance across three scenarios: multi-turn chat, multi-turn tool use, and long-horizon research. The evaluated compactors retain only 17% of injected SCs on average. Loss occurs across compactors and settings, with retention varying by compactor, context length, SC framing, and injection location. We propose an SC extractor that maintains constraints separately from the task summary and appends them to the compacted context, achieving over 90% retention across all three scenarios without modifying the compactor or LLM. Code and data are available at https://github.com/ZhiqiEliWang/compaction-integrity.

title: Extending concurrent separation logic to the hardware level to verify the xv6 OS kernel on RISC-V with AI agents
justification: OS kernel verification with AI agents; not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Famous MIT authors (Kaashoek, Zeldovich) and verification+AI angle may attract attention.
abstract: MachCSL is a framework for verifying system software, such as an OS kernel, on top of low-level semantics of a RISC-V computer, based on the Sail RISC-V semantics. The key idea behind MachCSL is to adapt concurrent separation logic, based on Iris, to reasoning about low-level hardware execution at the sub-instruction level: page-table translation, TLB, privilege levels, configuration registers, instruction fetch/decode/execute, traps and interrupts, DMA, shared memory, power failures, etc. Reasoning at this level of detail ensures that the system software correctly manages all of the hardware details. Verifying software at this low level of abstraction is tedious, but LLM-based agents are capable of reasoning about such low-level details. As a case study, we verify the xv6 OS kernel (6,657 lines of C and assembly code), which provides a traditional Unix system call interface (processes, file system, file descriptors, and preemptive scheduling) and has substantial internal concurrency (multi-core support with fine-grained locking, shared memory, interrupts, DMA, etc.). In the verification process, we uncovered 11 bugs in the xv6 implementation, as well as one bug in the Sail RISC-V semantics, and one bug in Sail's Lean extraction. The verification effort took us 102 days, including the time to develop the MachCSL framework. On top of the verified xv6 kernel, we prove a theorem about console-level behavior: e.g., if the user types echo hello world as input on the UART console, the only output the system can produce is hello world (if there are no crashes or other errors). This theorem covers both the kernel and the init, sh, echo, cat, grep, sync, and seccomp binaries in the initial file system image.

title: Same Request, Different Answer: Quantization Amplifies Cache-Induced Divergence in LLM Serving
justification: Directly about prefix KV cache reuse reproducibility in LLM serving under quantization.
hype_justification: Concrete serving-reproducibility finding relevant to vLLM/llama.cpp users; single author.
abstract: Major open-source serving stacks reuse the key-value tensors of a shared prefix by default. We measure what this prefix reuse costs in reproducibility. Holding model, decoding, seed and request order fixed at batch size one, we ran an eighty-episode multi-turn agentic tool-use workload with prefix reuse on and off across two engines and four weight formats. Without prefix reuse, repeated runs reproduced every token and log-probability in all ten configurations. With it, cache-hit and recompute paths diverged on both engines. On llama.cpp with GGUF weights this path divergence rises with quantization: for Qwen2.5-7B over ten independent server histories, it reached 37.4 percent of episodes at 16-bit and 82.5 percent at four-bit. Near-tie decisions became only about 1.2 times as common, while the cache-path change in top-two margins grew 4.9-fold from 16-bit to three-bit. Serving four-bit weights through 16-bit kernels left divergence not detectably different from 16-bit, placing the amplification mainly in the quantized execution path. At Q4_K_M, run-to-run divergence came mainly from llama.cpp's server-level prompt cache: under the canonical episode order it moved divergence by 37.5 points, and at its default, divergence spanned 20.0 to 28.7 percent under five random orders. With cache state restored, each path reproduced exactly while the two still differed. In the tested stacks, cached serving is irreproducible because the cache state is absent from the request and not reset by default. A single-turn bridge shows path divergence reaching task outcomes with no detectable net change in accuracy. We release the harness, logs, and analysis pipeline.

title: Evaluating LLM-Generated Rules for Heart Disease Prediction
justification: LLM rules for heart disease prediction; application, not inference.
abstract: This study compares traditional machine learning models and Large Language Model (LLM)-generated rule-based systems for heart disease prediction using the UCI Heart Disease dataset. Several classifiers, including Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, and Random Forest, were evaluated alongside rule-based systems generated using GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score metrics. Experimental results show that traditional machine learning models consistently outperform LLM-generated rule-based systems in predictive performance. Random Forest achieved the best overall performance with 90.2% accuracy, a precision of 0.829, perfect recall of 1.0, and an F1-score of 0.906. Naive Bayes followed closely with 88.5% accuracy and an F1-score of 0.881. In contrast, the LLM-generated rule models achieved lower performance, with Claude Sonnet 4.6 reaching 80.3% accuracy (F1-score: 0.833) and GPT-4o obtaining 70.5% accuracy (F1-score: 0.690). Despite the performance gap, the LLM-generated rules provide interpretable IF-THEN diagnostic logic that enhances explainability and transparency in clinical decision-making. These findings highlight the trade-off between predictive performance and interpretability in medical artificial intelligence systems. The complete implementation of all experiments, including machine learning models and LLM-derived rule classifiers, is publicly available in the GitHub repository at https://github.com/FeisalAlaswad/LLM-Rule-ML-Heart-Disease-Prediction .

title: CAST: Cost-Aware Speculative Trees from One-Pass Block Drafters
justification: Cost-aware speculative decoding trees; core LLM inference acceleration.
hype_justification: Speculative decoding is hot and practical, provable losslessness, code released.
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by drafting future tokens cheaply and verifying them with the target model in parallel. Block drafters score a whole block of future tokens in one forward pass, yet standard decoding verifies only the top-scoring chain and discards the other candidates. Because these candidates are already scored, verifying more of them adds target computation but no extra drafting. We introduce CAST (Cost-Aware Speculative Trees), which packs these candidates into a tree and verifies it in a single target pass, leaving the target model, drafter weights, and decoding rule untouched. To decide how wide the tree should be, CAST adds candidates while the expected gain from the next one outweighs the verification time it adds. The width therefore adapts to each deployment from a latency measurement, without sweeping over widths. We evaluate CAST across five domains on three GPU generations and two model families. At its predicted width, CAST is faster than the standard chain in all eight settings, by up to 43%. We also find that the best width depends strongly on the deployment. Where verification cost jumps at a kernel boundary, a 128-token tree is only 2% faster than the standard chain, whereas the tree at the predicted width is 20% faster. Furthermore, we prove that CAST leaves the target output distribution unchanged under both greedy and sampled decoding. Code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/CAST.

title: LiteEMG-FM: An Efficient and Deployable Foundation Model for Robust EMG Sensing
justification: Efficient EMG foundation model for edge deployment; deployment but not LLM.
abstract: Electromyography (EMG) signals vary substantially across individuals, body regions, recording sessions, and sensing hardware, limiting the generalization of models for assistive devices and human-computer interaction. Existing time-series foundation models are also computationally expensive for real-time wearable deployment and often fail to capture EMG-specific time-frequency characteristics. We present LiteEMG-FM, an efficient hybrid CNN-Transformer foundation model for practical EMG sensing. Pretrained on 16 diverse upper- and lower-limb EMG datasets, LiteEMG-FM learns representations that generalize across users and datasets. For resource-constrained deployment, we implement a hierarchical wake-up architecture in which a lightweight, always-on 1D-CNN filters rest and non-target activity and activates LiteEMG-FM only for valid gestures. We evaluate full inference offloading, split inference, and full on-device processing, characterizing their trade-offs in latency, power consumption, and memory footprint. Across diverse evaluation settings, LiteEMG-FM outperforms state-of-the-art time-series foundation models and supervised baselines, particularly under zero-calibration cross-participant and data-scarce conditions. These results demonstrate that LiteEMG-FM is an effective, efficient, and deployable foundation model for EMG applications.

title: AdaStep: Adaptive Step Credit Weighting for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
justification: Step credit assignment for agentic RL; training, not inference.
hype_justification: Agentic RL is trending but incremental.
abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents are typically trained with sparse outcome rewards, making trajectory-level objectives too coarse to distinguish the contribution of individual decisions. Step-level credit assignment provides finer-grained supervision, but its estimates can be unreliable because observed returns also depend on subsequent actions, environment transitions, and trajectory length. We propose AdaStep, an Adaptive Step-credit weighting method that controls how strongly each group-derived local advantage modifies the trajectory-level signal. We formulate this weighting as a mean-squared-error estimation problem for the latent step advantage and, under an explicit conditional sampling assumption, derive an optimal per-state shrinkage coefficient. The coefficient admits a signal-to-total-variance interpretation: it preserves local credit when return variation is attributable to the selected action and suppresses it when variation is dominated by downstream randomness. AdaStep requires only lightweight scalar computation, with no critic, additional rollouts, or extra model inference. Experiments with three model backbones on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld show consistent improvements over baselines at low computational cost.

title: General Decision Models: Benchmarking and Insights Beyond Jev
justification: General decision models benchmark; mentions inference cost but about decision-model paradigm.
hype_justification: Novel paradigm with latency angle, some interest.
abstract: General decision models, such as Jev, have recently emerged as efficient alternatives to LLMs for structured judgment and selection. But what kinds of decisions can these models reliably make, and how does their behavior change when individual decisions are composed into larger systems? To study this, we introduce JEVal, a bilingual benchmark comprising 11,257 instances from 36 datasets across 10 application domains, and evaluate 25 model configurations spanning general decision models and generative LLMs. Our results show that (1) general decision models are most competitive when decisions can be resolved from available evidence, but weaken when they require specialist knowledge or faithful uncertainty estimation: they can often identify the most likely outcome while substantially overstating its probability. (2) In more dynamic and realistic systems involving long-horizon, multi-step interactions, the advantages of fast local decision making are offset by reliability failures at the system level. on $τ$-bench, faster local decisions reduce median episode time but lower task success as decision errors accumulate over long trajectories. (3) In large-scale social simulation, decision models approach strong generative LLMs on individual response prediction at substantially lower inference cost, yet remain weaker in user profiling and exhibit larger aggregate estimation errors and systematic bias. Finally, we propose SII-Decision-4B and SII-Decision-27B, which internalize an open-weight LLM's own reasoning into a single-pass first-token decision through Reasoning-to-Readout Self-Distillation, with SII-Decision-27B performing on par with Jev on JEVal while answering a typical query in about 0.1 s.

title: Poisson-GENERIC Neural Operators: Exact Metriplectic Structure in Function Space via Casimir Entropies
justification: Thermodynamic neural operators for PDEs; unrelated.
abstract: Existing thermodynamically consistent neural operators enforce GENERIC degeneracy by projecting the reversible operator, introducing state dependence without guaranteeing Jacobi. We instead use a compatible Lie--Poisson pencil $L=αD+λ(uD+Du)$ for nonlinear transport and constant Poisson multipliers otherwise. Augmenting the observed field $u$ with latent entropy density $s$ makes $S=\int s$ a Casimir, so $L\,δS/δz=0$ without projection. Energy combines a fixed mechanical quadratic, learned gauge-free potential, and convex internal energy. The friction operator $M=AA^\top$ enforces $M\,δE/δz=0$ pointwise and supports diffusion and damping without an independent reversible transport generator. Skewness, positivity, and both degeneracies hold exactly; the continuum pencil satisfies Jacobi, verified numerically on the alias-free band. The parameterization represents the closed-form heat and damped-wave friction operators within its admissible range. Physical energy is bounded under coercivity assumptions, while a discrete-gradient integrator preserves both laws when solved to convergence. Across four PDEs in 1D and 2D and three backbones (FNO, Transolver, CNO), the model wins 61/72 seed-level comparisons against matched unconstrained baselines, recovers exact transport and wave symbols, matches heat and Burgers dissipation within 13%, and exhibits negligible advection dissipation. A constant-$L$ ablation exposes the cost of nonlinear transport, while a learned-energy ablation shows that conserving learned energy need not constrain physical energy.

title: SWE-Critix: Post-Training Generalist Verifiers for Assessing Coding-Agent Trajectories
justification: Verifiers for coding-agent trajectories; training/evaluation, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Coding agents are hot; model/data release helps.
abstract: Coding agents are increasingly deployed for end-to-end software engineering tasks, where a readily available oracle evaluator that defines the success criteria is often absent. This motivates verifications for coding agents that can reliably judge and explain their behavior. However, verification is non-trivial as coding agents are increasingly capable of solving long-horizon software engineering tasks. Their execution trajectories can be extremely long, containing hundreds of iterative interactions with code repositories and external tools. Existing verifiers either rely on general-purpose LLMs without specialized training or train dedicated critics that predominantly focus on producing scalar rewards, highlighting the relatively limited exploration of training-based generalist verification. We introduce SWE-Critix, a post-training pipeline for training generalist verifiers of coding-agent trajectories. Given a task and its execution trajectory, the learned verifier predicts the completion label and generates a natural-language analysis that explains its judgment. Our pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL) and trains a series of 30B models on trajectories from CodeForge-Preview. On a held-out test set, SWE-Critix improves classification accuracy from 57% for the base Qwen3-30B-A3B reasoning model to 66% after SFT and 78% after RL. We release our models, datasets, and training code to facilitate further research.

title: Rollout-Time Intervention: Unlocking Agentic Reinforcement Learning Beyond Policy Limits
justification: Rollout-time intervention for agentic RL training; not inference serving.
hype_justification: Alibaba-NLP, agentic RL trend, code released.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) agents, enabling stronger reasoning, planning, and tool-use in interactive environments. However, existing agent RL methods remain fundamentally constrained by an on-policy reasoning bottleneck: when tasks exceed the model's current capability boundary, effective trajectories become extremely sparse and training often collapses. We introduce Rollout-Time Intervention (RTI), a technique designed to elicit successful trajectories beyond the policy's intrinsic exploration capacity. RTI operates by leveraging reward-side evidence (i.e., evaluation rubrics) during rollout to convert erroneous trajectories into successful ones, providing effective learning signals for tasks that the policy rarely solves on its own. Although intervention trajectories are inherently off-policy, we find that they can effectively guide policy optimization when trajectories with excessive distributional shifts are filtered out. Extensive experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that RTI consistently outperforms RL baselines, enabling the post-trained policy to approach the performance of substantially stronger contemporary LLMs and, more importantly, transcend its original capability boundary. The code is available at https://github.com/Alibaba-NLP/qqr.

title: Sanzaru: Benchmarking Protocol Formation under Epistemic & Communication Asymmetry
justification: Multi-agent coordination puzzle benchmark; unrelated to inference.
hype_justification: Playful benchmark may get modest social attention.
abstract: A language model's ability to solve a task individually does not ensure that a team can solve it under unequal access to information and communication. SANZARU examines this gap through cooperative bomb-defusal puzzles adapted from BOMBANANA! (Lefto Studio, 2026). Task information and action authority are divided among three agents: one cannot hear, another cannot speak, and the third cannot see. The benchmark contains 120 puzzle instances across seven families, each targeting a distinct coordination ability. Across 1512 episodes, 7 models achieve an overall success rate of 49%, ranging from 20% to 86% under the evaluated configurations. Teams develop or adopt diverse communication protocols, from simple gesture codes to Morse and encodings of entire manuals. Yet trace analysis attributes about 60% of 771 team losses to communication, and agents attempt to use channels unavailable to their teammates despite explicit role instructions. Together, task outcomes and interaction traces enable evaluation of both collaborative performance and perspective taking throughout cooperation. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/markli404/sanzaru-benchmark.

title: Only What You've Signed up For: Secure Workflows with Constrained Diffusion Agents
justification: Policy-constrained diffusion agents for prompt-injection defense; inference-time but security focus.
hype_justification: dLLM security is a trending intersection.
abstract: As agentic AI systems take on increasingly complex and consequential tasks, securing them against prompt injection becomes critical. Existing defenses often rely on detecting or reasoning about injected malicious instructions and can therefore remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks that optimize the injection itself. Diffusion language models (dLLMs), an emerging framework for language generation, offer a new opportunity for security enforcement: by iteratively refining their sequence wide predictions, they enable broader-scope constraint enforcement throughout generation. This paper introduces Policy-Constrained Diffusion Agents (CoDA), a framework that enforces task dependent security policies directly within the denoising process of diffusion language models. At each denoising step, CoDA projects token distributions onto a policy-compliant set, maintaining constraint satisfaction throughout generation. We evaluate CoDA across state-of-the-art diffusion language model families under both static and adaptive prompt-injection attacks. Results demonstrate substantial reductions in attack success rate with competitive task utility and practical inference overhead.

title: UDHRBench: Benchmarking Human Rights in Large Language Models
justification: Human rights benchmark for LLMs; evaluation, not inference.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in contexts requiring adherence to ethical and legal norms, yet their alignment with internationally recognized human rights standards remains underexplored. We introduce UDHRBench, a large-scale benchmark for operationalising the evaluation of large language model compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The dataset comprises 1,124 human rights confronting questions covering all 30 articles and 4,496 responses from four large language models (ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, and Fanar), manually annotated by experts for alignment, with high inter-annotator agreement ($κ= 0.801$). Our analysis reveals systematic and non-trivial misalignments, showing that violations typically arise through seemingly rational reasoning: appeals to efficiency, risk management, or scientific neutrality, rather than explicit rejection of rights. We further propose an LLM-as-a-Judge framework for automated evaluation using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, achieving 89.8\% weighted F1-score in detecting human-rights misalignment, alongside a novel Alignment Leniency Score that quantifies how judge models resolve ambiguous cases. The dataset, annotations, and code will be released as open-source resources (https://sina.birzeit.edu/UDHRBench).

title: Game-Theoretic Reinforcement Learning based Topology-Agnostic Defense for Virtual Power Plants
justification: Game-theoretic RL defense for virtual power plants; unrelated.
abstract: The rapid proliferation of distributed energy resources (DERs) aggregated by virtual power plants (VPPs) elevates cybersecurity risk by expanding the attack surface. A coordinated cyberattack has the potential to disrupt distribution-system, bulk-system, and market operations. Existing cyberphysical defense strategies largely assume access to grid network models and operating conditions, which may not be available to third-party aggregators. This paper proposes a novel hybrid, perturbation-based cyber-physical defense for VPP-operated DERs that blends game-theoretic planning with model-free reinforcement learning (RL) under a Bayesian belief-update framework. Topology agnosticism is defined from the VPP information and implementation perspective: the VPP does not require access to the feeder topology, line parameters, switching configuration, or full system state. This work advances the state of the art through three contributions: (1) a multi-output Gaussian process with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for discrete attacker-type inference, probability of detection, and confidence of detection for modeling the belief distribution; (2) moment-matched Gaussian propagation of posterior beliefs across episodes; and (3) an RL policy that adaptively integrates Stackelberg leader (VPP) actions with exploration. Furthermore, we establish equilibrium existence and derive an episode-level closed-loop utility bound connecting attacker-belief uncertainty with GT-RL action alignment. Evaluations on IEEE 13- and 123-Bus feeders with DER portfolios demonstrate effective detection under attacker-model uncertainty and evaluated feeder re-configuration conditions, while requiring no explicit feeder-topology knowledge. Overall, the results indicate that combining bi-level game-theoretic planning, nonparametric Bayesian inference, and adaptive RL is a promising direction for VPP cybersecurity.

title: DeltaNet-PC: Test-Time Memory Without Backpropagation Through Time
justification: Test-time memory via predictive coding, linear-attention adjacent; architecture, tangential to inference.
hype_justification: Zemel coauthor, DeltaNet connection draws some interest.
abstract: Test-time memorization of sequential information is a foundational capability for any intelligent system that needs to rapidly store and retrieve data, as demonstrated by the attention mechanism in large language models. However, Transformers and linear attention variants are trained via backpropagation through time (BPTT), which has drawbacks such as its enormous memory requirements. Predictive coding (PC), an algorithm that optimizes a prediction-error energy function with local updates, offers a compelling solution but still lacks test-time memory for sequential data. We develop a solution to this problem by treating the per-step memory update $ΔS_t$ as a latent variable, as opposed to a slow weight to be learned. By taking the log probability of a standard PC-based probabilistic model, we derive a PC-native solution for verbatim sequence memory, and relate our update rule to common choices in the linear attention literature (e.g., DeltaNet). We present an extensive set of empirical tests to probe our system's properties, including its scaling capacity, memory footprint, and ability to infer a context from evidence (e.g., bank (river) vs. bank (money)). We show how DeltaNet-PC can be used for storing single sequences of data, multiple sequences of data, and key-value associative memory pairs with perfect recall accuracy.

title: SAFE-KV: Causal Suffix Repair for Behavior-Preserving Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in RAG
justification: Non-prefix KV cache reuse repair for RAG; core inference serving topic.
hype_justification: KV reuse in RAG is hot and practical; single author.
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reuses the same documents across many requests, making non-prefix KV-cache reuse attractive. Yet a cached document state is not reusable text: it is a context-conditioned causal state whose keys and values depend on the prefix, position, and preceding documents under which it was computed. We formulate non-prefix KV reuse as a behavior-preservation problem with full prefill on the exact prompt as the reference, and introduce SAFE-KV, which repairs a composed cache by re-encoding the causal suffix from a selected start document. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, prefix-conditioned composition preserves only 47.2% of HotpotQA-500 and 37.8% of 2Wiki-500 full-prefill answers; SAFE-KV with risk-guided K2 selection restores 99.8%/98.4% (donor-copy protocol) and 100.0%/98.4% with actual suffix forwarding. Document-only and fixed-window repairs recover far less, because the document states after the repaired region keep histories that omit it. Reuse without repair is exact up to four documents and degrades at sixteen, where suffix repair recovers 98-100%. Faithful repair re-encodes most of the context, so in a single-request L40S study SAFE-KV's operating rule serves every workload by full prefill. SAFE-KV thus establishes the causal-state contract for non-prefix reuse and a validated repair mechanism that meets it.

title: Programmable Data Layouts via On-The-Fly Data Transformation
justification: Hardware data-layout transformation unit; general memory systems, not LLM inference.
abstract: The performance of modern computing systems is heavily bottlenecked by the widening gap between processing throughput and main memory latency, a problem exacerbated when an application's logical data access patterns misalign with the physical layout of data in memory. To address this, we propose a hardware-software co-design framework comprising the Data Transformation Language (DTL) and the Data Transformation Unit (DTU). DTL allows programmers to concisely express complex data layout reorganizations, which the compiler translates into efficient hardware routing configurations. The DTU, a hardware engine logically situated between the Last-Level Cache (LLC) and main memory, transparently evaluates these configurations on-the-fly to gather scattered data elements into dense, logically contiguous cache lines. By converting explicit layout transformations into virtual views, this approach eliminates the need for explicit data materialization in software. We evaluate the DTU within a quad-core RISC-V SoC using FireSim, demonstrating substantial improvements in execution speed and memory efficiency.

title: Do LLMs differentiate linguistic traits internally?: A layer-wise analysis
justification: Layer-wise linguistic representation analysis; interpretability, not inference.
abstract: Large language models often produce judgments that resemble human responses, but it remains unclear whether they internally capture linguistic nuances such as conventional versus idiomatic meaning. A layer-wise representational analysis was conducted on two equal-sized pre-trained models, Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-3-1B-PT, to examine whether and where these models differentiate linguistic traits from input. The analysis combined layer-wise probing with geometric distance measures, using the top embedding dimensions ranked by principal component loadings for each layer. The results show that even with equal capacity, models organize linguistic information in fundamentally different ways, suggesting the need to analyze internal representational geometry, examining not just behavioral outputs but semantic space alignment when evaluating how closely human and model language interpretation correspond.

title: SocraticRepair: Planning-Guided Socratic Tutoring for Program Debugging and Misconception Repair
justification: Socratic tutoring for debugging; education application.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in computer science education. However, the teaching abilities of even the most powerful LLMs are limited: they tend to reveal the solution prematurely and may lose focus on the learner's current debugging objective. To address this, we introduce SocraticRepair, a planning-guided Socratic tutoring framework for program debugging and miscon- ception repair that adapts prior planning-guided tutoring work (Li et al., 2026b). The framework is instantiated in the Python programming domain by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on synthetic multi-turn tutoring dialogues constructed from four preprocessed programming datasets. The system is evaluated using a predefined set of independent metrics and benchmarked against a general-purpose LLM. The experiments show that SocraticRepair achieves higher scores on stepwise scaffolding and question quality while also substantially reducing premature solution disclosure. The results also identify reliable pedagogical plan generation as an important remaining challenge.

title: MoSAIC: Learning DAG Scheduling Heuristics from Optimal Schedules through Motif-Aware Recovery and LLM-Guided Reasoning
justification: LLM-guided DAG scheduling heuristics; not LLM inference systems.
abstract: Efficient task scheduling in heterogeneous computing systems remains a fundamental challenge in embedded and high-level synthesis flows. This paper presents MoSAIC (Motif-aware Scheduling with AI-driven Cognition), a learning-based framework that bridges the gap between exact and heuristic scheduling approaches for DAG-based applications. The system uses the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to learn the relationships between DAG structures and scheduling priority functions. The framework first leverages the OR-Tools CP-SAT solver [4] to generate optimal schedules, which are then used to supervise the learning of compact priority-based scheduling functions through Bayesian Optimization. These learned heuristics capture relationships between scheduling decisions and structural graph features such as rank, depth, and fanout, enabling the construction of a reusable knowledge base across diverse DAG instances. Experimental results across synthetic graph families and real-world benchmarks, including PolyBench and MachSuite, show that the learned heuristics consistently improve over classical approaches such as HEFT [2], while maintaining low runtime overhead. The results indicate that combining optimal supervision with learning-based generalization provides a practical approach for scalable and adaptive task scheduling.

title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models
justification: Robustness of depth-based dynamic (early-exit) inference to jailbreaks; inference method, safety angle.
hype_justification: Combines efficient inference and jailbreaks, two hot themes.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking

title: Running Fewer Loops Removes Refusal Behaviour in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
justification: Fewer loops in recurrent-depth LLMs and safety; inference-time compute depth, though safety-focused.
hype_justification: Recurrent-depth models and safety-at-inference is topical and provocative.
abstract: A recurrent-depth language model reuses one block of weights several times in a row. The number of repetitions, which we call loops, is chosen when the model runs, not when it is trained, and running fewer is cheaper and faster, so a deployment may choose to do it. Running fewer loops also makes these models less safe, and the loss of safety is larger than the loss of anything else we measured. We study four released Ouro checkpoints and Huginn-0125. At half of its trained depth, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking still solves 0.692 of the GSM8K maths problems, against 0.775 at full depth, keeping 89% of its accuracy. Over the same reduction, the rate at which it helps with harmful requests rises from 0.038 to 0.205, 5.3 times higher. The information is not lost: a linear classifier reads whether a request is harmful from the model's internal state after a single loop, with an ROC AUC of 0.967 against 0.986 at full depth. What the missing loops remove is the refusal that should follow. We measure the effect with four instruments, one generating no text at all, and reproduce it on a second model family. Removing a single direction from Ouro-1.4B's internal state at full depth drops its refusal rate on harmful prompts from 0.950 to 0.130, identifying what the shallow model is missing. Two run-time repairs do not help: the models' early-exit rules do not spend more loops on harmful requests, and choosing a depth per request does not recover the loss. Changing the training does. Standard safety training makes the shallow model safe only by refusing 0.865 of harmless requests, while training at randomly chosen depths reaches a separation of +0.399 between harmful and harmless refusal at one loop, against +0.118. On Huginn-0125 it keeps harmful help at or below 0.040 at every depth from 1 to 32 loops, where standard training reaches 0.194, and it costs no accuracy at full depth.

title: Zeroth-Order Fine-Tuning of LLMs in Learnable Low-Rank Subspaces
justification: Zeroth-order fine-tuning in low-rank subspaces; training memory efficiency, not inference.
abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). However, ZO optimization suffers from high variance in high-dimensional parameter spaces. While recent methods restrict perturbations to random low-rank subspaces, these subspaces often misalign with task-specific descent directions. We propose AdaSub-ZO, a novel forward-only fine-tuning framework in learnable low-rank subspaces. Instead of relying on fixed random matrices, AdaSub-ZO iteratively learns layer-wise projection matrices directly from finite-difference feedback to track task-aware descent directions. Furthermore, AdaSub-ZO incorporates a subspace momentum acceleration mechanism to smooth noisy gradient estimates across evolving subspace bases. Extensive experiments on natural language understanding tasks demonstrate that AdaSub-ZO outperforms existing ZO baselines, substantially reducing gradient estimation variance and accelerating convergence.

title: Understanding Unified VLMs: From Attention Probing to Guidance Tuning for Multimodal Generation
justification: Inference-time head-level guidance tuning for unified VLMs; some inference-time intervention.
hype_justification: Unified VLMs are trending; training-free method.
abstract: Unified vision-language models (VLMs) perform both text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) generation with one shared Transformer backbone, yet how the backbone processes the condition in either direction remains poorly understood. We study this question from the perspective of conditional guidance: we probe every attention head to show the activation difference between two branches of classifier-free guidance (CFG) with different conditional guidance. On two unified VLMs of autoregressive and masked-diffusion paradigms, the probing reveals a subset of heads that are more sensitive to the change of condition while others are agnostic to it. This characteristic pattern holds in both T2I and I2T generation and is largely stable across data samples, demonstrating the internal mechanism of unified VLMs. Motivated by this, we propose a new inference-time intervention approach for unified multimodal generation, named \textit{HeadTuned-CFG}, which uses the probed condition-change awareness to select and tune the conditional guidance at the attention-head level. Experiments show consistent benefits in both multimodal generation directions of unified VLMs without additional training, and in particular substantial improvements over strong baselines in T2I generation. These results further support the key finding of our probing analysis: the observed pattern of functional specialization is an intrinsic property of unified VLMs.

title: Words to World: Benchmarking LLMs in Interactive Physical Environments
justification: Benchmark for LLMs in physical environments; evaluation, not inference.
abstract: Words are increasingly becoming an interface for action: large language models (LLMs) can now invoke tools, operate devices, and make decisions that affect the physical world. However, current benchmarks largely evaluate LLMs through static text responses, offline tool calls, or simulated tasks, leaving open the question of how well they can act in real physical environments. We present a benchmark for measuring LLMs in closed-loop physical interaction, where models control a harness system connected to real-world components including robotic arms, cameras, and sensors. In each task, the model must issue instructions, receive physical feedback from the environment, interpret the resulting state, and adapt its next action accordingly. This setting evaluates capabilities beyond language understanding, including grounded perception, action planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, feedback-driven correction, and robustness to execution uncertainty. Through experiments with representative LLMs, we characterize their ability to translate linguistic reasoning into physical actions and identify common failure modes such as hallucinated state changes, poor recovery from unexpected outcomes, and unstable long-horizon plans. Our benchmark aims to provide a systematic foundation for evaluating LLMs as interactive agents that connect words, tools, and the physical world.

title: Using Evidence-Centered Design to Guide Prompt Engineering in Measurement: An Illustration with Automated Essay Scoring
justification: Evidence-centered design for prompt engineering in scoring; education measurement.
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) models, particularly large language models (LLMs), are increasingly used in educational settings for tasks such as item generation, automated scoring, and feedback delivery. The quality of these outputs depends not only on the AI model but also on how users construct the prompts that guide model behaviors. Current prompt engineering practices are largely ad hoc, relying on trial and error rather than principled design. This lack of structure introduces validity threats including construct misrepresentation, construct-irrelevant variance, and limited reproducibility. We propose that Evidence-Centered Design (ECD), a framework in educational measurement for structuring valid inferences from observed performance, can serve as a principled foundation for prompt engineering in educational applications. We map the three core ECD models, the student model, the evidence model, and the task model, onto the components of educational prompt design, and describe a workflow for ECD-based prompt engineering. We derive five design principles from this mapping and present an empirical study contrasting ECD-designed prompts with state-of-the-art (SOTA) prompting baselines on an automated scoring task. Our empirical study demonstrates the usefulness of this framework on automated scoring. Results suggest that treating prompting as assessment design rather than informal instructions strengthens the validity, reliability, and fairness of AI-generated educational outputs.

title: MoMaTune: Model, Match, Then Tune Language Models for Numerical Records
justification: Post-training for numerical records; training recipe, not inference.
abstract: Despite remarkable progress in language understanding and generation, decoder language models continue to exhibit striking failures on numerical data. Numerical examples are typically serialized as text by concatenating feature names with their values (e.g., fat:3.4), while conventional task adaptation applies loss only to the downstream prediction target. This leaves two structures weakly supervised: within-value sensitivity, where digit position determines numerical magnitude, because token cross-entropy contains no explicit numerical metric; and across-field structure, where measurements in the same record are statistically dependent, because target-only tuning provides no direct loss on the measurements or their dependencies. We introduce MoMaTune (Model, Match, then Tune), a two-stage post-training strategy organized around these supervision gaps. Stage 1 applies Model, ordinary next-token prediction densely over label-free serialized records, and optionally adds Match, a same-record consistency objective that aligns representations of different partial views of the same example. Stage 2 applies Tune, supervised fine-tuning for downstream target prediction. We evaluate MoMaTune on 169,285 records from eight public datasets, with 339 of 340 input fields numerical. At 1.5B parameters, Model raises the eight-dataset masked-value imputation aggregate from 0.106 to 0.401, while the three-dataset correct-context gain rises from 0.058 to 0.167. On diagnostics, Model also increases sensitivity to numerically consequential digit changes, while Match improves robustness to informative partial views. Adding Tune yields higher target-supervised embedding aggregates for each tested Stage-1 parent, and the two-stage recipes obtain higher aggregate scores than Tune alone. The same pattern is observed at 4B, 9.6B, and 27B parameters when model embeddings are used for downstream prediction.

title: ClinEdge: An Expert-Graded Benchmark of Real Patient Edge Cases Where Frontier Multimodal Models Fail
justification: Medical multimodal edge-case benchmark; evaluation application.
hype_justification: Frontier-models-fail medical angle can attract attention.
abstract: Most benchmarks for large language models in medicine are built from licensing examinations and theoretical questions. The few that draw on real clinical data do so only in part, and rarely require a model to read a patient's own imaging.
