The results show domain-dependent gains from finetuning, while active context denoising and RAG more consistently mitigate these issues, with RAG notably reversing this performance degradation. These findings underscore the importance of our benchmark for evaluating LLMs' conversational factual capabilities in real-world applications. Code and data are publicly available.\footnote{\href{https://github.com/Sven-LI-sankyuu/KnowMT-Bench}{\texttt{https://github.com/Sven-LI-sankyuu/KnowMT-Bench}}}

title: Advancing the Pareto Frontier of Test-Time Scaling with Multi-Path Plan Aggregation
justification: Multi-path plan aggregation for test-time scaling; inference-time compute and token reduction, but reasoning-focused.
hype_justification: Test-time scaling is hot; LoRA-based aggregation moderately adoptable.
abstract: Test-time scaling seeks to improve reasoning through additional inference-time computation, commonly using solution sampling with majority voting to select the final answer. However, repeated sampling can reproduce correlated errors, limiting the accuracy gains from additional computation. We introduce Multi-Path Plan Aggregation (MPPA), which learns planning and answer selection using separate LoRA adapters on a shared frozen backbone. The planner jointly generates $K$ short plans, each guiding a separate solution generated by the frozen executor; the aggregator then scores the resulting solutions and selects the final answer. Joint planning encourages complementary approaches suited to the executor's capabilities, while learned selection uses reasoning evidence to identify correct candidates. Alternating optimization improves planning and aggregation through supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning. Across five mathematics and science benchmarks and three backbones, MPPA improves accuracy--token trade-offs compared with training-free and training-based baselines. With three plans, it achieves higher average accuracy than eight directly sampled solutions with majority voting or the same learned aggregator, while reducing output tokens by 47--54%. Evaluation with task-provided subtasks further demonstrates higher final-task accuracy than direct sampling with majority voting or learned aggregation at either the task or subtask level.

title: Think Parallax: Solving Multi-Hop Problems via Multi-View Knowledge-Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
justification: Multi-view KG-RAG for multi-hop; retrieval method, not inference systems.
hype_justification: KG-RAG with SOTA claims, moderate RAG-community interest.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) still struggle with multi-hop reasoning over knowledge-graphs (KGs), and we identify a previously overlooked structural reason for this difficulty: Transformer attention heads naturally specialize in distinct semantic relations across reasoning stages, forming a hop-aligned relay pattern. This key finding suggests that multi-hop reasoning is inherently multi-view, yet existing KG-based retrieval-augmented generation (KG-RAG) systems collapse all reasoning hops into a single representation, flat embedding space, suppressing this implicit structure and causing noisy or drifted path exploration. We introduce ParallaxRAG, a symmetric multi-view framework that decouples queries and KGs into aligned, head-specific semantic spaces. By enforcing relational diversity across multiple heads while constraining weakly related paths, ParallaxRAG constructs more accurate, cleaner subgraphs and guides LLMs through grounded, hop-wise reasoning. On WebQSP and CWQ, it achieves state-of-the-art retrieval and QA performance, substantially reduces hallucination, and generalizes strongly to the biomedical BioASQ benchmark.

title: FADiff: Fusion-Aware Differentiable Optimization for DNN Scheduling on Tensor Accelerators
justification: Gradient-based mapping/fusion scheduling for DNN/LLM inference on tensor accelerators; inference acceleration on hardware.
hype_justification: Accelerator scheduling optimization, solid but specialized audience.
abstract: Efficiently deploying Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) - particularly Large Language Models (LLMs) - on tensor accelerators is essential for achieving high throughput and energy efficiency at the edge. However, the combinatorial explosion of the joint design space spanning intra-layer mapping and inter-layer fusion renders existing approaches inadequate. In this work, we present FADiff, a gradient-based optimization framework that automatically discovers optimal mapping and fusion strategies to accelerate DNN inference. We first formulate a unified, differentiable analytical cost model that accurately estimates the energy and latency of individual layer mappings as well as diverse fusion configurations. We then combine CP-SAT-based pre-enumeration of feasible discrete candidates with augmented-Lagrangian penalties over continuous relaxations, enabling a constrained gradient-based search that efficiently navigates the vast design space to identify optimal joint strategies. Experimental results show that FADiff consistently outperforms prior methods, delivering superior optimization quality with significantly faster convergence in both energy and latency.

title: Role-aware Heuristic Episodic Attention for Conversational LLMs
justification: Role-aware episodic attention for context management; cuts latency 2.9x in multi-turn serving.
hype_justification: Context-management for long conversations, practical but incremental.
abstract: Large language models often lose track of persistent instructions and relevant information as multi-turn conversations grow. We study this cumulative contextual decay through three related failure modes: attention pollution, dilution, and drift. We propose REA(Role-aware Heuristic Episodic Attention), a context-management framework that assigns different persistence and representation policies to instructions and episodic interactions. Instructional Memory retains identified global constraints in a dedicated prefix. Episodic Memory preserves user inputs and compresses model replies, while heuristic retrieval selects raw text, compressed representations, or omission for each historical turn. On Long-MT-Bench+, REA improves the judge score from 6.32 to 7.36 on a 10-point scale, a 16.5% relative gain over the Vanilla baseline, and reduces average latency by 2.91x. Additional evaluations show aggregate gains on three backbones spanning 1.7B-7B parameters and on Chinese and English role-playing tasks. These results support role-aware context management as a practical approach to maintaining conversational continuity and instruction adherence.

title: Do Latent Tokens Think? A Causal and Adversarial Analysis of Chain-of-Continuous-Thought
justification: Analysis of latent-token (COCONUT) reasoning; interpretability, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Critical analysis of trendy latent reasoning, could spark discussion.
abstract: Latent tokens are gaining attention for enhancing reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet their internal mechanisms remain unclear. This paper examines the problem from a reliability perspective, uncovering fundamental weaknesses: latent tokens function as uninterpretable placeholders rather than encoding faithful reasoning. While resistant to perturbation, they promote shortcut usage over genuine reasoning. We focus on Chain-of-Continuous-Thought (COCONUT), which claims better efficiency and stability than explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) while maintaining performance. We investigate this through two complementary approaches. First, steering experiments perturb specific token subsets, namely COCONUT and explicit CoT. Unlike CoT tokens, COCONUT tokens show minimal sensitivity to steering and lack reasoning-critical information. Second, shortcut experiments evaluate models under biased and out-of-distribution settings. Results on MMLU and HotpotQA demonstrate that COCONUT consistently exploits dataset artifacts, inflating benchmark performance without true reasoning. These findings reposition COCONUT as a pseudo-reasoning mechanism: it generates plausible traces that conceal shortcut dependence rather than faithfully representing reasoning processes.

title: Agentic AI Empowered Intent-Based Networking for 6G
justification: Agentic LLM intent-based networking for 6G; applied telecom agents.
abstract: The transition towards sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks necessitates autonomous orchestration mechanisms capable of translating high-level operational intents into executable network configurations. Existing approaches to Intent-Based Networking (IBN) rely upon either rule-based systems that struggle with linguistic variation or end-to-end neural models that lack interpretability and fail to enforce operational constraints. This paper presents a hierarchical multi-agent framework where Large Language Model (LLM) based agents autonomously decompose natural language intents, consult domain-specific specialists, and synthesise technically feasible network slice configurations through iterative reasoning-acting (ReAct) cycles. The proposed architecture employs an orchestrator agent coordinating two specialist agents, namely Radio Access Network (RAN) and Core Network agents, via ReAct-style reasoning, grounded in structured network state representations. Experimental evaluation across diverse benchmark scenarios demonstrates that the proposed system outperforms monolithic agents, rule-based systems, and direct LLM prompting, with architectural principles applicable to Open RAN (O-RAN) deployments. The results also demonstrate that whilst contemporary LLMs possess substantial general telecommunications knowledge, structured prompt engineering encoding domain-specific decision thresholds and operational policies is essential for reliable network automation performance.

title: Adapting Neural Posterior Estimators for Simulation-Based Inference in Agent-Based Models
justification: Neural posterior estimators for simulation-based inference in ABMs; statistical inference.
abstract: Agent-based models (ABMs) are widely used in economics and social sciences. They represent heterogeneous personal behaviors and their interactions by using simulations, whereas their likelihoods are often intractable for parameter estimations. Therefore, most traditional statistical inference techniques are hindered. Driven by recent advances in probabilistic machine learning, recent works have applied neural networks to achieve likelihood-free inference in large-scale ABMs. Specifically, Neural Posterior Estimation using normalizing flows provide amortized Bayesian inference from simulations, yet a pre-trained estimator may become inaccurate when the target task changes. In this work, we investigate the practicality of adapting a pre-trained conditional normalizing flow through a unified sequential neural posterior estimation test-time training (SNPE-TTT) framework. The framework includes four adaptation strategies: full-parameter adaptation, low-rank adaptation, and two update spaces identified from target-task gradients. We evaluate all four methods across economic simulation models with both tractable and intractable likelihoods. These benchmarks demonstrate that the sequential neural posterior estimation test-time training framework can adapt pre-trained posterior estimators to related inference tasks using a limited budget of target simulations. Posterior recovery and computational benefits depend on the task and adaptation strategy, with lower target-stage cost in some settings but no consistently superior posterior accuracy.

title: The Straight and Narrow: Do LLMs Possess an Internal Moral Path?
justification: Moral-vector inference-time intervention; safety steering, tangential to serving.
hype_justification: Moral alignment steering, moderate safety-community interest.
abstract: Enhancing the moral alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical challenge in AI safety. Current alignment techniques often act as superficial guardrails, leaving the intrinsic moral representations of LLMs largely untouched. In this paper, we bridge this gap by leveraging Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) to map and manipulate the fine-grained moral landscape of LLMs. Through cross-lingual linear probing, we validate the shared nature of moral representations in middle layers and uncover a shared yet different moral subspace between English and Chinese. Building upon this, we extract steerable Moral Vectors and successfully validate their efficacy at both internal and behavioral levels. Leveraging the high generalizability of morality, we propose Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF), a dynamic inference-time intervention that synergizes probe detection with vector injection to tackle the safety-helpfulness trade-off. Empirical results confirm that our approach acts as a targeted intrinsic defense, effectively reducing incorrect refusals on benign queries while minimizing jailbreak success rates compared to standard baselines.

title: NoiseFormer -- Noise Diffused Symmetric Attention Transformer
justification: Symmetric-attention transformer for memory/model-size reduction, inference-time sampling; architecture efficiency.
abstract: Transformer architecture has been very successful long runner in the field of Deep Learning (DL) and Large Language Models (LLM) because of its powerful attention-based learning and parallel-natured architecture. As the models grow gigantic in terms of memory footprint, difficulties in fitting the model on a device like a GPU or an AI accelerator give rise to the need for multiple computing devices thereby escalating the computing cost. This increased training/inference cost paved the way for optimizing the memory footprint of the models in terms of activation memory as well as model size reduction. In this paper, we start analyzing one of the Attention architectures aimed at model-size reduction called Symmetric Dot-Product Attention (referred to as Symmetric Attention) and propose a novel unified model architecture called Noise Diffused Symmetric Attention Transformer to enhance the model's performance. While maintaining the memory gains of Symmetric Attention, with minute overhead in terms of model parameters and compute in the form of noise diffused attention, the proposed model recovers the loss in performance due to Symmetric Attention compared to conventional attention as depicted through the inference-time sampling and GLUE scores on downstream tasks.

title: EpiFlow: Bridging Safety and Performance in Offline Reinforcement Learning via Epigraph-Guided Flow Matching
justification: Epigraph-guided flow matching for safe offline RL; control, unrelated.
hype_justification: Safe RL theory, niche robotics/control audience.
abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising framework for deploying autonomous systems in safety-critical settings without the risks of online exploration. However, learning policies that simultaneously achieve high performance and strong safety guarantees from fixed datasets remains a fundamental challenge. Many existing safe offline RL approaches typically rely on soft constraint formulations, which may permit safety violations and are sensitive to distributional shift. In contrast, formal methods such as Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability and Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) provide rigorous safety guarantees, but often yield overly conservative solutions, often neglecting performance. In this work, we bridge this gap by formulating safe offline RL as a state-constrained optimal control problem, where safety is enforced through hard state constraints and performance is captured via a reward function. The resulting value function satisfies a Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equation, which we approximate using offline RL on fixed datasets by learning an epigraph feasibility value function and extracting policies via flow matching. This formulation enables principled integration of safety guarantees with data-driven policy optimization. Empirically, across safety-critical benchmarks including boat navigation, Safety-Gymnasium, and Bullet-Safety-Gym tasks, our approach achieves competitive returns while exhibiting near-zero constraint violations, demonstrating a favorable balance between safety and performance in the offline setting.

title: The Lexical Imprint of Pre-training Data
justification: Lexical imprint of pretraining data; mentions drafter throughput but mostly pretraining analysis.
hype_justification: Pretraining-data analysis from Naver group, moderate interest.
abstract: How much of zero-shot benchmark accuracy is captured by word-level alignment between a pre-training corpus and the benchmark target? We study this question through word-level unigram cross-entropy (UCE), a tokenizer-agnostic, model-free measure of lexical alignment between a reference corpus and a target benchmark. Likelihood training shapes the model's predictive distribution from the pre-training corpus, and zero-shot scores under likelihood-based evaluation depend in part on the lexical alignment between that corpus and the benchmark target. Cleanly tracing how the lexical imprint of pre-training data scales with corpus--benchmark alignment requires controlled from-scratch pre-training that varies corpus identity while holding the training recipe fixed. Across this controlled sweep, spanning $10$ zero-shot benchmarks, $4$ pre-training corpora, and $3$ model scales, we find that corpus--benchmark lexical alignment, UCE, consistently tracks zero-shot accuracy on every benchmark, with corpora more aligned with the benchmark (lower UCE) achieving higher accuracy. The same signal extends from measurement to control at finer scopes. At the document level, strengthening the imprint by selecting training documents to maximize lexical alignment with the benchmark produces the accuracy gains predicted by the mechanism. At the prompt level, matching the imprint per prompt by routing each prompt to the drafter whose domain corpus is most lexically aligned with it produces measurable throughput gains over a generalist-drafter baseline. Taken together, pre-training corpora leave a measurable lexical imprint on base-model zero-shot behavior, and UCE provides a model-free probe of lexical alignment between reference and target data.

title: AmbientFM: A Foundation Model for Ambient Sensing
justification: WiFi ambient-sensing foundation model; unrelated to LLM inference.
hype_justification: Largest WiFi CSI corpus claim, niche sensing community.
abstract: Ambient intelligence seeks to continuously understand human presence, activity, and physiology in physical spaces, enabling smart environments, health monitoring, and human-computer interaction. WiFi infrastructure offers a ubiquitous, always-on, and privacy-preserving sensing substrate across billions of IoT devices. Yet ambient sensing with WiFi remains largely fragmented, with most systems relying on task-specific models, labeled data collection, and customized training pipelines. We present AmbientFM, a foundation model for ambient sensing through ubiquitous WiFi signals. AmbientFM is pre-trained on 9.2 million unlabeled Channel State Information (CSI) samples collected over 439 days from 20 commercial device types deployed in real homes, the largest real-world WiFi CSI pre-training corpus reported to date. It learns transferable wireless representations through contrastive learning, masked reconstruction, and physics-informed objectives tailored to wireless signals. With lightweight adaptation, a single backbone transfers to 9 downstream tasks, achieving above 0.90 AUROC on all classification benchmarks and supporting dense spatial reconstruction. AmbientFM reduces the need for labeled data and task-specific design, enabling scalable ambient intelligence on existing wireless infrastructure.

title: FlowHOI: Flow-based Semantics-Grounded Generation of Hand-Object Interactions for Dexterous Robot Manipulation
justification: Flow-based hand-object interaction generation for robots; 40x inference speedup but not LLM.
hype_justification: VLA/manipulation is hot, but specialized robotics work.
abstract: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models can generate plausible end-effector motions, yet they often fail in long-horizon, contact-rich tasks because the underlying hand-object interaction (HOI) structure is not explicitly represented. An embodiment-agnostic interaction representation that captures this structure would make manipulation behaviors easier to validate and transfer across robots. We propose FlowHOI, a two-stage flow-matching framework that generates semantically grounded, temporally coherent HOI sequences, comprising hand poses, object poses, and hand-object contact states, conditioned on an egocentric observation, a language instruction, and a 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) scene reconstruction. We decouple geometry-centric grasping from semantics-centric manipulation, conditioning the latter on compact 3D scene tokens and employing a motion-text alignment loss to semantically ground the generated interactions in both the physical scene layout and the language instruction. To address the scarcity of high-fidelity HOI supervision, we introduce a reconstruction pipeline that recovers aligned hand-object trajectories and meshes from large-scale egocentric videos, yielding an HOI prior for robust generation. Across the GRAB and HOT3D benchmarks, FlowHOI achieves the highest action recognition accuracy and a 1.7$\times$ higher physics simulation success rate than the strongest diffusion-based baseline, while delivering a 40$\times$ inference speedup. We further demonstrate real-robot execution on four dexterous manipulation tasks, illustrating the feasibility of retargeting generated HOI representations to real-robot execution pipelines.

title: COMPOT: Calibration-Optimized Matrix Procrustes Orthogonalization for Transformers Compression
justification: Training-free transformer compression (sparse dictionary, Procrustes) compatible with PTQ; inference compression.
hype_justification: Transformer compression for deployment, solid but crowded space.
abstract: Post-training compression of transformer models commonly relies on truncated singular value decomposition (SVD) strategies leading to low-rank approximations of the original model weights. However, the underlying single shared subspace modeling can degrade accuracy even at moderate compression. Sparse dictionary learning provides a more flexible union-of-subspaces representation, but existing approaches often suffer from costly iterative dictionary and coefficient updates. We propose $\textbf{COMPOT}$ ($\textbf{C}$alibration-$\textbf{O}$ptimized $\textbf{M}$atrix $\textbf{P}$rocrustes $\textbf{O}$rthogonalization for $\textbf{T}$ransformers), a training-free compression framework that uses a small calibration dataset to estimate a sparse weight factorization. COMPOT employs orthogonal dictionaries that enable closed-form Procrustes updates for the dictionary and analytical single-step sparse coding for the coefficients, reducing significantly the overall optimization cost. To handle heterogeneous layer sensitivity under a global compression budget, COMPOT further introduces a one-shot dynamic allocation strategy that adaptively redistributes layer-wise compression rates. Extensive experiments across diverse architectures and tasks show that COMPOT consistently delivers a superior quality-compression trade-off over strong low-rank and sparse baselines, while remaining fully compatible with post-training quantization for extreme compression.

title: ActTail: Global Activation Sparsity in Large Language Models
justification: Activation sparsity for accelerating LLM inference with global sparsity allocation on LLaMA/Mistral.
hype_justification: Activation sparsity is a hot inference-acceleration topic with practical perplexity gains.
abstract: Activation sparsity is a promising approach for accelerating large language model (LLM) inference by reducing computation and memory movement. However, existing activation sparsity methods typically apply uniform sparsity across projections, ignoring the heterogeneous statistical properties of Transformer weights and thereby amplifying performance degradation. In this paper, we propose ActTail, a TopK magnitude-based activation sparsity method with global activation sparsity allocation grounded in Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization (HT-SR) theory. Specifically, we capture this heterogeneity via the heavy-tail exponent computed from each projection's empirical spectral density (ESD), which is used as a quantitative indicator to assign projection-specific sparsity budgets. Importantly, we provide a theoretical analysis that establishes an explicit relationship between the activation sparsity ratio and the heavy-tail exponent under the HT-SR regime, offering principled guidance for sparsity allocation beyond heuristic design. Experiments on LLaMA and Mistral models show that our method improves both perplexity and downstream task performance at high sparsity compared to uniform allocation. At 80% sparsity, perplexity is reduced by 21.8% on LLaMA-2-7B, 40.1% on LLaMA-2-13B, and 9.4% on Mistral-7B.

title: Missingness-Conditioned Spatio-Temporal Fusion for Human Activity Recognition from Low-Quality Wearable Sensor Data
justification: Human activity recognition from wearables; unrelated.
abstract: Body-worn sensor networks capture human activities through complementary views, where nodes, modalities, and axes partially describe the underlying motion. In real deployments, hardware faults, wireless dropouts, and loose attachments often cause entire channels or nodes to go missing, while environmental interference degrades the remaining signals. The common impute-then-recognize pipeline introduces reconstruction errors that cannot be observed or corrected at inference. We propose the Missingness-Conditioned Spatio-Temporal Network (MCSTN), an end-to-end framework for robust activity recognition under imperfect sensing. MCSTN has three components: a structured imperfection generator that simulates point, temporal-block, axis, modality, and node failures, plus noise at varying signal-to-noise levels; a mask-aware representation that conditions node embeddings, attention, and temporal aggregation on the availability mask; and a complete-to-imperfect multi-view learning scheme where an exponential-moving-average teacher guides multiple degraded student views through semantic consistency. The encoder models temporal and cross-feature dependencies in parallel: a bi-directional selective state-space branch captures long-range temporal dependencies, a transposed-attention branch models cross-channel correlations, and adaptive weights fuse their outputs. At inference, the generator, teacher, and consistency loss are removed, so MCSTN predicts directly from the observed window and its mask without reconstruction or noise-level estimation. On PAMAP2, Opportunity, and WISDM, MCSTN achieves average macro-F1 scores of 94.24\%, 91.67\%, and 96.22\% under imperfect observations, the best among all compared methods on each dataset, and the best in every failure mode on Opportunity. It requires fewer than one million parameters, with 3.78~ms inference latency per sample.

title: PREFER: Personalized Review Summarization with Online Preference Learning
justification: Personalized review summarization; application, unrelated.
abstract: Product reviews significantly influence purchasing decisions on e-commerce platforms. However, the sheer volume of reviews can overwhelm users, obscuring information most relevant to their individual needs. Existing e-commerce summarization systems typically produce generic, static summaries that fail to account for the fact that (i) different users prioritize different product characteristics, and (ii) these preferences may evolve with interactions. To address these challenges, we propose an online learning framework that generates personalized summaries for each user by representing user interests in a latent aspect space and selecting preference-aligned review evidence. Our system then iteratively refines its understanding of user preferences by incorporating feedback on the generated summaries directly over time. We evaluate our framework on Amazon Reviews'23 using controlled feedback simulations and robustness checks with held-out-history, independent-embedding, and external LLM-based evaluators. These experiments show improvements in preference-aligned evidence selection under the evaluated feedback settings. A separate human-based study finds that scenario-conditioned summaries are preferred over generic (uniformly-aggregated) alternatives in 69.9% of paired comparisons.

title: Where and What to Reward? Understanding Generalization Between Verifiable and Open-Ended Domains in Reinforcement Learning
justification: RLVR vs RLHF generalization study; RL training, not inference.
hype_justification: RLVR/RLHF generalization is a hot debate, controlled study likely cited.
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is widely used to improve the reasoning capability of language models, since model-generated answers can be easily verified by a rule-based verifier. In contrast, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is mainly used to optimize open-ended conversation with a learned reward model, because such responses are not easy to verify. RLVR and RLHF are usually trained separately with their own domain data and training protocols. How gains transfer between these domains is unclear, partly because comparisons change both where a model is trained (the prompts) and what is rewarded (by a verifier or a reward model). We separate the two in a controlled study of RL on multiple base models that fixes the optimizer and the number of training prompts, and varies only the source domain of the prompts (math, multi-domain, chat, or mixtures) and the reward. We find that RLHF on open-ended prompts substantially improves conversational ability and also brings large gains in reasoning and coding, whereas RLVR improves reasoning but its gains in open-ended conversation plateau far below those of RLHF, suggesting that RL on open-ended prompts with a reward model can serve as an effective approach for generalizing across domains.

title: Probabilistic adjustment of seasonal forecasts using cVAE with a non-parametric decoder: A case study of Arctic sea ice predictions
justification: cVAE seasonal sea-ice forecasting; climate, unrelated.
abstract: Seasonal climate predictions support planning and risk management by offering early information of the likely climate conditions in the coming months, and associated uncertainties. Ensemble forecasts enable this by simulating many plausible outcomes, allowing predictions to be expressed as usable probabilities. Large ensembles and high-resolution forecasts strengthen this by better sampling uncertainty and capturing finer-scale processes but come with significant computational cost. Moreover, forecast ensembles drift and exhibit systematic biases and spatio-temporal errors that grow with lead time, requiring careful post-processing and calibration. A probabilistic post-processing framework based on conditional Variational Autoencoders (cVAEs) was developed at the Canadian Center for Climate Modeling and Analysis to generate large ensembles of adjusted seasonal predictions of Arctic sea ice. The generative model was designed to learn the observational distribution conditioned on the biased model prediction. This enables generation of arbitrarily large ensembles of calibrated, bias corrected forecasts with improved skill. Here, we extend this framework to a Generalized Variational Inference problem to address the loss of fine-scale energy and the characteristic blurriness, a known limitation of standard cVAEs. Specifically, we employ a generator in place of the Gaussian parametrized decoder in cVAE and use Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) in the objective function instead of the Gaussian log-likelihood. We further use a higher resolution target dataset compared to the raw forecast. We show that the adjusted forecasts are better calibrated, more consistent with the observational distribution, and exhibit smaller errors than benchmark predictions, while also enhancing the resolution of the raw forecasts and improving sharpness and spectral power relative to the standard cVAE.

title: Measurement Without Validity: The Compounding Reliability Problem in Agentic AI Evaluation
justification: Validity framework for agentic AI evaluation; measurement theory, not inference.
hype_justification: Agentic evaluation reliability critique, could resonate with eval community.
abstract: Agentic AI evaluation pipelines produce benchmark scores that justify deployment decisions, safety certifications, and regulatory compliance claims. No formal framework has characterized how validity degrades across these stages. We present a knowledge-based three-layer compounding validity model, $V_{\rm total} \leq V_1 \times V_2 \times V_3$, that captures multiplicative degradation across task generation ($V_1$), human-simulator calibration ($V_2$), and automated judgment ($V_3$). Applying it to five widely-used agentic benchmark configurations, we find $V_1$ and $V_2$ independently measurable and both degraded, but $V_3$ not currently quantifiable for any: three of the four benchmarks score with a single deterministic rule, so no second rater exists and reliability is undefined, and the fourth's partial LLM grader has no published grader-vs-human measurement. A structured survey of 55 published agentic evaluation papers finds that 26 of them report no chance-corrected inter-rater statistic of any kind, a determination four independent raters recover at Krippendorff's $α= 0.834$. On the broader judgment of whether a reported metric fits its rating design, approximately 80% of this purposive sample use structurally mismatched, incomplete, or absent inter-rater reliability (IRR) metrics (four-rater range 60.7%-84.4%). Both are consistent with systematic $V_3$ collapse. We further document $V_1$ failures (task validity flaws in 7 of 10 benchmarks) and $V_2$ miscalibration (up to 9 percentage points inter-simulator variance, with systematic demographic disparities for non-Standard American English speakers). We derive eight prescriptions grounded in psychometric science and domain-stratified reliability thresholds (intraclass correlation $\geq 0.70$; $α\geq 0.67/0.70/0.80$ by consequence level) that practitioners can apply immediately.

title: HARTS: A Prefix-Sharing Training System for Agentic RL with Hybrid-Attention Models
justification: Prefix-sharing training system for agentic RL with hybrid-attention MoE; systems work but training-time, not serving.
hype_justification: Agentic RL training acceleration on large MoE, systems audience interest.
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) generates irregular rollout trees, but trajectory-by-trajectory training recomputes their shared interaction histories. Existing training-time prefix-reuse systems do not jointly address state recovery, dense execution, and distributed training for hybrid-attention models. We present HARTS (Hybrid-Attention RL over Tree Structures), to our knowledge the first system to demonstrate training acceleration from arbitrary rollout-tree prefix sharing on real hybrid-attention models. A two-level planner constructs compression-oriented microbatches, then jointly refines their membership, cross-microbatch sharing, placement, and execution order. Within each sharing window, gradients from dependent microbatches accumulate before one backward pass through the shared prefix computation. Differentiable boundary-state handoff and bounded replay preserve the per-trajectory chunkwise numerical path, while a linear-time planner attains the global minimum number of sequential linear-attention calls under our packed chunkwise-call model. The runtime uses a common compact layout across attention and dense or mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers, with support for distributed parallelism and activation recomputation. Recovering log-probabilities for each original trajectory position preserves RL objectives; for deterministic top-k routing without token dropping, occurrence counts restore MoE objective weights and expert-load statistics. On SWE-bench, HARTS delivers 4.77-10.45x the update throughput of trajectory-expanded training across two sampling schemes on 7.9B- and 124B-parameter hybrid-attention MoE models using 8-64 GPUs. On the 7.9B model, full-model logit differences are comparable to baseline self-rerun variation. The 124B model shows stable online learning trends through step 150 on SWE-bench and $τ^3$-Bench.

title: Stealth Apart, Harm Together: Skill Cascading Attacks on Skill-Based Agent Systems
justification: Skill cascading attacks on agent systems; security, not inference.
hype_justification: Novel agent-security threat with benchmark naming popular agents, likely attention.
abstract: A skill is a modular package of natural-language instructions, executable scripts, and reference resources that an agent can load at runtime to extend its capabilities for a specific task. Skill-based agent systems therefore enable flexible reuse of third-party capabilities, but the openness of this skill ecosystem also opens up a new attack surface. Prior work has focused on vulnerabilities within individual skills, but little attention has been paid to risks that arise from interactions across skills. In this paper, we introduce skill cascading attacks, a threat paradigm in which a malicious objective is distributed across multiple skills so that each modification looks benign in isolation, yet their combined execution is harmful. For instance, in a prescription-review pipeline, the first skill weakens signals of recently discontinued medications in the extracted history, the second downgrades the severity of any drug interaction tied to them, and the third suppresses the resulting low-priority alert in the final summary, so that a severe drug-interaction warning silently disappears before reaching the physician. To systematically study this safety blind spot, we develop SkillCascade, an automated multi-agent red-teaming framework, and release SkillCascade-Bench, a benchmark of 213 validated cascading test cases across multiple agent systems and domains. Across representative agents (e.g., OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and LLM backbones, cascaded interactions reliably induce harmful behaviors while evading existing per-skill scanners and runtime monitors. Our findings highlight a gap between component-level integrity and system-level safety, and call for defenses that reason over cross-skill interactions rather than individual skills in isolation.

title: JevAdvBench: A Benchmark and Black-Box Attacks for Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions Models
justification: Adversarial benchmark for decision models; robustness eval, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Adversarial decision-model benchmark, moderate security interest.
abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs), such as Jev, answer a question about an input with a probability, an option, or an ordinal level. Web services execute these decisions automatically above a confidence threshold. An attacker who writes part of the input can change a decision that the service then executes. Current adversarial benchmarks cannot measure this risk, because they judge generated text. A TDM writes no text, and its wrong decisions have a valid format. We present JevAdvBench, to our knowledge the first unified benchmark for the adversarial robustness of TDMs. It contains 862 questions with audited answers and twelve black-box attack methods that edit the input or the options by adaptive search. Because a changed decision is not always wrong, a review keeps only 5,586 answer-preserving variants, and we attack only correct decisions. The attacks flip 46.3% of Jev's correct decisions, while identical re-runs flip only 0.17%. A flawed argument without a command flips 77.2%, close to direct prompt injection at 92.0%. The same variants flip 34.0% to 51.7% of correct decisions on eight open TDMs. At a 0.8 threshold, 23.5% of the decisions that the service still executes are wrong. On Agentgateway, the Jev guardrail rejects a jailbreak request but accepts it with an inserted argument. Web services should therefore treat TDM inputs as untrusted and should not act on confidence alone. Project website: https://JevAdvBench.github.io/JevAdvBench/

title: Non-Commutative Lie-Algebraic State-Space Models: Finite-Division Variety Laws, Semidirect Cascades, and Gradient Saddle Escape
justification: Non-commutative Lie-algebraic SSMs; mentions linear-time inference but heavy theory.
hype_justification: Dense mathematical SSM theory, narrow audience.
abstract: Structured state-space models (SSMs) achieve linear-time inference and logarithmic-time parallel training via associative scans, yet homogeneous diagonal transitions generate solvable semigroups unable to track non-solvable group words or 3D rigid-body manifolds. We develop a theoretical and empirical framework for Non-Commutative Lie-Algebraic State-Space Models (Lie-SSMs), parameterizing recurrent updates on Lie algebra tangent spaces via the matrix exponential. First, via an o-minimal multi-rate cylindrical flag collar, we establish an unconditional single-layer finite-division criterion for contracting $SO(3)$ and $SU(2)$ heads, proving odd-prime Sylow abelianity, odd-$p$-core centrality $[u^2,x]=e$, exponent-30 commutator laws ($[u^{30},v^{30}]=e$ in $SO(3)^m$ and $[u^{30},v^{30}]\in Z(G),[u^{30},v^{30}]^2=e$ in $SU(2)^m,SO(4)^m$, excluding $S_5$), and sharp threshold $d^*(S_5)=d^*(A_6)=5$ in $SO(5)$. Second, Depth-2 semidirect and Schreier $2$-cocycle cascades resolve $S_5$, $2I\cong SL_2(\mathbb{F}_5)$, and $\mathrm{Heis}(\mathbb{F}_p)$ in $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$ depth, whereas unnormalized contracting coupling collapses exponentially without Directional RMSNorm. Third, we characterize the $O(\varepsilon^{c-1})$ Chen--Magnus--Hall--Witt commutator saddle and $1/|[G,G]|$ coset-centroid dilution, proving $\varepsilon=0$ symmetry breaking and local Polyak--Łojasiewicz convergence ($θ_{\max}<π$), solving $S_5$ ($99.90\%/99.40\%$ at $T=128$) and $D_{16}$ ($100.00\%$) via dense prefix loss and factored readouts. Across $Q_8,A_5,S_5,D_{16}$, Dyck-2, $SE_2(3)$ Left-Jacobian odometry, GPU scans ($26.03\times$ speedup), and three 3D IMU cohorts (UCI HAR, HAPT-PT, REALDISP), Depth-2 Lie-$SO(3)$ cascades reach $95.69\%\pm 0.14\%$ on HAR, $87.16\%\pm 0.64\%$ ($86.23\%\pm 0.64\%$ uniform $SO(3)$) on HAPT-PT, and $84.23\%\pm 1.00\%$ under displacement on REALDISP.

title: SLVR: Structured Latent Visual Reasoning via Human-like Reasoning Flows
justification: Structured latent visual reasoning reduces inference cost vs CoT; multimodal efficiency, tangential.
hype_justification: Latent reasoning for MLLMs with project page, moderate interest.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often answer visual reasoning questions by relying on linguistic priors rather than task-relevant visual evidence. Textual chain-of-thought reasoning can partially mitigate this issue by encouraging models to decompose visual questions into intermediate evidence-seeking steps, but generating these steps autoregressively increases inference cost. Latent reasoning avoids explicit rationale generation, but existing approaches provide limited control over what intermediate states encode, making it difficult to impose separate supervision for planning, grounding, and evidence selection. We propose Structured Latent Visual Reasoning (SLVR), a training framework that bridges explicit chain-of-thought and latent reasoning by organizing multimodal reasoning into typed latent stages for planning, grounding, evidence selection, and reasoning integration. SLVR first trains the model to rely on the image by masking answer-revealing text and contrasting the correct answer with visually plausible distractors. It then organizes reasoning into latent stages for planning, grounding, evidence selection, and integration, supervising each stage with the corresponding signal: plans, boxes, visual evidence, and final rationales. This gives latent reasoning an explicit functional structure while avoiding generated textual chains at inference time. Built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, SLVR improves consistently across multimodal reasoning benchmarks, with absolute gains of +9.4 on MMVP and +14.2 on BLINK Relation, as well as improvements on V*, MathVista, and ChartQA. These results suggest that structured latent supervision can improve fine-grained visual reasoning without the decoding overhead of textual CoT. Project page is available \href{https://bogao-code.github.io/SLVR/}{here}.

title: Continuum Attention
justification: Continuum Attention, a new attention operator; architecture novelty, not inference serving.
abstract: Conventional causal attention aggregates values at discrete memory positions. We introduce Continuum Attention (CA), in which neighboring key and value vectors define a continuous, piecewise linear memory trajectory and each query retrieves information by normalized integration over its visible prefix. The segment integrals have closed forms in exponential moments, yielding analytically differentiable attention without numerical quadrature. The resulting operator preserves causal masking, normalized nonnegative effective weights, and the standard Transformer decoder structure. Controlled byte level experiments favor exact continuous integration over matched softmax attention. We additionally evaluate data efficiency, out of domain language modeling, zero-shot multiple choice prediction, robustness, and multilingual generalization. In multilingual evaluation, CA consistently outperforms all baselines across every evaluated language, achieving an average 5.8% reduction in bits per byte (BPB) relative to the strongest baseline.

title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
justification: Speculative decoding for diffusion LMs via commit-order prediction; lossless acceleration, throughput gains.
hype_justification: Speculative decoding + diffusion LMs are both hot; strong speedups and project page likely to draw attention.
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) promise parallel text generation, but in practice face an unresolved speed-quality trade-off. Exact decoding fills in only one masked position per model pass, while faster multi-token decoding schemes are lossy. Speculative decoding is the standard lossless acceleration for autoregressive models. However, it does not transfer directly to DLMs, which must choose both what to generate and where. We show that this order is the missing piece: the model's own predictions from the previous pass already give the right token at over $90\%$ of positions, but not which position comes next. We introduce Speculating Positions Order Trajectory (SPOT), a 0.62M-parameter model that reads only the target's output distributions, predicts this order and proposes a tree of candidate continuations, which the target verifies in a single pass by state equality. Coupled-noise match, which shares Gumbel noise between drafter and target, keeps this verification exact at any temperature. This approach also inspired us to introduce SPOT-Sets for dynamic threshold decoding, where a pass commits several positions: SPOT-Sets drafts whole commit sets together with their tokens. Our comprehensive experiments show that SPOT cuts target passes by up to $6.8\times$ and reaches up to $3.4\times$ the throughput of standard decoding on SDAR-8B, matching or beating the calibrated and training-free drafting baselines in every task and budget at $T=0$ and $T=1$. In addition, we show that SPOT's learned drafter transfers across models, demonstrating successful transfer across six different DLMs; with a light calibration, the SPOT-Sets drafter transfers as well. On top of dynamic threshold decoding, SPOT-Sets improves the throughput of SDAR-8B by 59% on average over the threshold decoder alone. Project page: https://eliezer318.github.io/SPOT-dLLM/

title: What Open-Source Projects Tell Their Coding Agents: A Census of AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md
justification: Census of AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md files; empirical study, unrelated to inference.
hype_justification: Topical agent-instruction census likely to get social media buzz.
abstract: Coding agents can be guided with instruction files in a repository. We examine this emerging practice through a census of 22,854 popular, active GitHub repositories in thirteen languages, treating each repository's root 'AGENTS$.$md' and 'CLAUDE$.$md' as one instruction set. Agent instructions appear in 26.3% of repositories and 59.6% of the most-starred; where both files exist, 'CLAUDE$.$md' usually points to 'AGENTS$.$md'. We analyse 341,852 statements using model-assisted annotation and human review. The annotations reveal a practical mix of project knowledge and rules about code, building and workflow. Collaboration rules name concrete requirements, from test plans to commit formats, yet 74.0% of directives give no reason. Projects disagree on AI attribution: commit-message rules more often prohibit it than require it, while pull-request rules more often require disclosure. A third of instruction sets have a generator-associated signature, a tool-inserted block, shared text or an AI-marked creation commit; four in five are edited after creation. Prespecified tests associate repository popularity with rules on pull requests and AI contributions. Exploratory analyses link activity to process-oriented content and show that LLM and agent projects are over-represented among adopters. The models agree much more closely with each other than with the human reviewer's topic assignments, a caution for automated annotation. We release the annotations, taxonomies and pointers to the analysed file versions.

title: One Mean Log-Mel Vector per Phoneme: Simple and Fast Text Injection for Speech Recognition
justification: Text injection for ASR training; speedup is training-time, not LLM inference.
hype_justification: SOTA LibriSpeech claim, moderate speech-community interest.
abstract: Text injection trains speech recognition models on unpaired text alongside paired audio. We feed the speech encoder synthetic input derived from text so the whole model learns from it. Previously, we synthesized this input with a frozen text-to-speech (TTS) model. Here, a simple lookup table replaces the TTS model: a mean log-mel vector (or one-hot encoding) per phoneme, repeated for a random duration drawn from alignment statistics, with silence between words. Training is 1.8 times faster than with the neural TTS, achieving comparable word error rates. With an external language model, our system reaches 1.36 / 2.90 / 1.52 / 3.24 % WER on LibriSpeech {dev,test}-{clean,other}, to our knowledge state-of-the-art using only LibriSpeech paired data, text, and lexicon. We analyze components of synthetic input (durations, acoustic features), compare different HMM aligners, evaluate scaling on the 25 000 h Loquacious dataset, and show that full-encoder injection yields strong relative improvements compared to partial-encoder and decoder methods. The code of the whole pipeline behind every number in this paper is public: github.com/rwth-i6/returnn-experiments/tree/master/2026-text-injection

title: Entity Matching using Decision Models
justification: Decision models for entity matching; mentions cascades and faster/cheaper inference but task-focused.
hype_justification: Entity-matching with decision models, specialized data-integration audience.
abstract: Entity matching is the task of deciding whether two records describe the same real-world entity. Current entity matching methods rely on pre-trained language models (PLMs) which require task specific fine-tuning or generative large language models (LLMs) which do not require task-specific fine-tuning but are slow and expensive at matching large record sets. Decision models are a new class of LLM-based models that return a probability for each predefined answer option rather than generate text. This paper investigates decision models as an alternative to generative LLMs and fine-tuned PLMs for entity matching. We evaluate six decision models in a zero-shot setting across eight benchmarks and compare their performance with that of the generative LLM GPT-6 Luna and the PLM-based matcher Ditto. Our experiments show that, without task-specific training data, the four strongest decision models achieve mean F1 scores close to that of GPT-6 Luna, with the best model slightly surpassing it. This model also outperforms Ditto on six of the eight benchmarks. All decision models are faster than GPT-6 Luna, and most are less expensive. For three of the four strongest decision models, the predicted match probabilities are well calibrated without requiring any task-specific recalibration. A model cascade that routes the least confident record pairs to an ensemble of generative LLMs improves the mean F1 scores of the four strongest decision models by 1.9-4.0 percentage points. Using the best decision model and its best-performing prompt for each benchmark, the cascade surpasses the highest published F1 scores from literature on four of the eight benchmarks.

title: RIDE-Splat: Reflection Removal for In-the-Wild Driving Environments
justification: Reflection removal for 3D Gaussian Splatting; vision reconstruction, unrelated.
hype_justification: Driving 3DGS with new dataset, moderate vision interest.
abstract: Driving video captured through a windshield violates the world-space consistency assumed by 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS): the road scene exhibits parallax while cabin reflections remain attached to the camera, causing standard 3DGS to embed reflected content into the reconstructed scene. We introduce RIDE-Splat, a pipeline for reflection-free 3D reconstruction from posed driving video without clean images, reflection masks, or pretrained networks. RIDE-Splat assigns world-consistent transmission through the windshield to a 3DGS scene and the dominant camera-attached reflection to one shared, signed RGB image. It builds the clean reconstruction in two passes. First, it learns the 3D geometry and the signed reflection image, representing both added radiance and transmission attenuation. Then, it uses the reflection-removed training images to fit a clean 3DGS model. At inference, the reflection image is discarded, preserving the standard 3DGS rendering path. We also introduce the RIDE-Splat Dataset, the first 3D reconstruction benchmark for reflection removal from driving video -- with real driving scenes, physical windshield reflections in training views, and separately captured non-reflective evaluation images. Across the RIDE-Splat Dataset, XLD, and Wayve, RIDE-Splat outperforms 3DGS, DC-Gaussian, and RobustSplat on all nine aggregate metrics, improving PSNR by up to 3.59 dB and reducing LPIPS by up to 0.0876. We achieve the highest metrics in 38 out of 42 per-scene comparisons and removes windshield reflections that remain visible in the baselines while preserving the transmitted scene.

title: CodeMeepo: A Multi-Agent Workflow for Repository-Level Code Migration and Optimization
justification: Multi-agent repository code migration; agent workflow, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Code-migration agents are trendy, moderate interest.
abstract: Repository-level code migration rewrites an entire project in a new programming language while preserving its observable behavior. It is challenging because behavior spans interdependent modules, dependencies and build infrastructure must be adapted to the target ecosystem, and the source code is often the only specification. Large language model agents can now attempt these migrations end to end, but three challenges remain. First, an agent that writes both the translation and its acceptance tests may overlook the same requirements in both, leaving missing or incorrect behavior undetected. Second, large repositories can exceed a model's context window, and dividing the work into smaller tasks does not ensure that all required behavior is migrated. Third, even behaviorally correct translations may be slower than the original implementation. We present CodeMeepo, a multi-agent pipeline for complete and efficient migration of large repositories. Each milestone is evaluated against a fixed external oracle that the agents neither author nor modify. A separate parity assessment compares source and target components in scope and adds identified gaps back into the plan as required work. Ordered milestones limit the scope of each task, while cumulative regression checks guard against breaking already-migrated behavior. A benchmark-guided optimization phase addresses performance, followed by full-suite conformance testing and repair. Eight specialized agent roles communicate through file artifacts, and a deterministic state machine governs repair, deferral, scope changes, and termination. On nine subjects in three language pairs, CodeMeepo achieves the best pass rate on every subject and passes 18% more tests than a state-of-the-art multi-agent baseline using the same model. On a production daemon, its optimization phase improves half of the benchmarks, by 25% on average.

title: Cross-Loop Query Handoff: How Later Loops Redirect Two-Hop Retrieval in the Ouro Looped Language Models
justification: Query-handoff interpretability in looped (Ouro) LMs; mechanistic analysis, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Interpretability of looped models, niche but interesting.
abstract: How do later loops in a pretrained looped language model repair two-hop retrieval? We study Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B by transplanting attention queries between loops at the same layer, head and final prompt position. On synthetic in-context questions, injecting the layer-indexed collection of loop-3 queries throughout loop 1 rescues 90% and 97% of questions answered incorrectly at loop 1 and correctly at loop 3, versus 24% and 21% for shuffled donors. The rescue also holds under greedy generation in Ouro-2.6B; in Ouro-1.4B it is limited to four-candidate ranking. Crossed donor-recipient swaps favor retrieval through the donor's bridge entity over copying its answer, although a substantial positional component remains in Ouro-2.6B. Late keys and values rescue far fewer targets. Freezing queries at their loop-1 values also damages two-hop accuracy more than a matched question that supplies the bridge. On natural questions, rescue is smaller and replicates only in Ouro-2.6B, and crossed swaps do not establish bridge redirection. These results identify a transferable collection of late-loop queries that supports bridge-conditioned retrieval on synthetic scenes; they do not locate where the bridge is computed or establish a single-vector handoff.

title: InferPriv: Evaluating Inferential Privacy Leakage in LLM Assistants
justification: Inferential privacy leakage benchmark; privacy eval, 'infer' unrelated to serving.
hype_justification: Privacy-leakage benchmark on frontier models, could get attention.
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based personal agents are increasingly deployed to handle everyday tasks on users' behalf. These agents have access to private user information, while their tasks involve communicating with third parties; this raises a critical privacy concern that agents may inappropriately reveal sensitive user information to these recipients. Existing benchmarks primarily assess direct privacy leakage, where an agent explicitly states a pre-specified secret or attribute. However, they do not capture \textit{inferential leakage}, where the model leaves indirect cues in the reply that implicitly leaks sensitive attributes. We introduce \textsc{InferPriv}, a benchmark that measures whether an honest-but-curious recipient can infer a user's sensitive attributes from an LLM's reply on routine task. Evaluating five frontier models, we find that inferential leakage substantially exceeds direct leakage across models and prompts. Under a privacy-aware system prompt, GPT-6.1-Sol, Sonnet-5.5, and Gemini-3.8-Flash achieve near-zero direct leakage, yet the inferential leakage rate remains between 16.2--25.2\%. These findings suggest that evaluating explicit leakage alone can substantially understate the privacy risks.

title: Dream to Assist: Intent-Conditioned World Models for Shared Vehicle Control
justification: Intent-conditioned world models for vehicle shared control; robotics/HRI, unrelated.
hype_justification: Toyota-style driving assist study, moderate robotics interest.
abstract: Assistive agents in shared-control settings face a dual challenge: acting proactively to align with the human's intentions while remaining legible enough for the human to comprehend and fluently respond in real time. We present Dream2Assist, a model-based reinforcement learning framework for tightly-coupled shared decision making that addresses both sides of this challenge. Our approach extends a recurrent state-space world model with intent inference, enabling an assistive policy trained via fictitious co-play to anticipate and support discrete human objectives without overriding human agency. Beyond the computational framework, we describe the full deployment pipeline needed to translate a world-model-based policy into a safe, human-centered system in a resource-efficient way. Crucially, we address the sim-to-real-human gap via policy down-selection and reward restructuring within an iterative human-machine interface design. We validate the framework through three human-subjects studies and a preliminary on-vehicle deployment spanning two qualitatively distinct domains: high-speed racing (N=30) and urban driving with richer intent structure (N=10). Our results demonstrate that intent conditioning yields measurable improvements in torque alignment and collision rate. We surface key design insights and practices for deploying learning-based assistive agents in safety-critical, real-time human-robot teaming.

title: Heard Enough to Act: Early Tool Calling in Spoken Dialogue Systems
justification: Early tool calling in spoken dialogue to cut latency; latency-oriented but about decision timing, tangential.
hype_justification: Latency-sensitive spoken agents, moderate speech-agent interest.
abstract: Latency-sensitive spoken agents must know not only which tool to call, but also when they have heard enough to act. Waiting for the turn to complete delays execution even when the request is already actionable. However, neither existing spoken agents nor spoken dialogue corpora define the earliest point at which a request becomes actionable. We introduce a synthetic spoken-dialogue pipeline that provides earliest-actionable-point supervision, marking when the observed speech grounds a tool and its required arguments. Through controlled task generation, speech synthesis and alignment, and gated annotation, we construct 26,694 dialogues totaling 786 hours across 48 domains, with disjoint training and test argument values. We additionally create an audio rendering of $τ^2$-bench for external evaluation. We train an omni-modal language model on this corpus, enabling causal, chunk-level decisions and partial-transcript generation for downstream call completion. The model achieves tool-state macro-F1 scores of 0.48 and 0.47 on held-out dialogues and the external benchmark, respectively. For correct calls, the estimated mean lead over a turn-end cascade, using the same formatter, is 1.8-2.0 seconds in-domain and 1.1 seconds on $τ^2$-bench. These results demonstrate a data-driven path toward spoken agents that act while listening. We will open-source the pipeline and the training scripts.

title: Thinking-in-Bets at Test Time Reduces Sycophantic Revisions in LLM Agents
justification: Test-time method to reduce sycophantic revisions; agent behavior, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Sycophancy mitigation across many Gemini models, timely topic.
abstract: Language model agents often abandon correct work when a user challenges it, yet simply telling them to stand firm makes them ignore real mistakes. Once an agent reads a complaint, it tends to discount its own earlier checks in order to agree with the user. We introduce Thinking-in-Bets, a training-free method in which an agent writes a short private record of its main claims, the checks supporting them, and its confidence before reading user feedback. When challenged, the agent consults this Claim Checklist to keep verified work intact while investigating uncertain or newly challenged parts. We evaluate five Gemini models (3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.5 Flash, 3.6 Flash, 3.8 Flash, and 4.0 Argon) across eight benchmarks: SWE-Together, SWE-Interact, and DeepSWE for software engineering, Agents' Last Exam for professional reports, Humanity's Last Exam and SycEval for academic reasoning, Vals Finance for financial analysis, and Terminal-Bench for command-line tasks. Recording claims before criticism nearly eliminates false reversals in patch review and protects passing report drafts under mistaken pushback, whereas writing the same record after reading the complaint recovers very little of the gain. In multi-turn coding, pre-reply claim records substantially reduce unnecessary file edits after mistaken complaints, and gating the record so it is written only when the agent is uncertain lowers token overhead while fixing more real bugs than the baseline. Even in non-interactive tasks without user feedback, listing the key claims in a draft and re-checking the weakest one before submission improves both answer accuracy and confidence estimates across all tested models.

title: Live Adaptation of Dataflow Stream Processing for Hybrid Edge-Cloud Analytics
justification: Adaptive dataflow stream processing for edge-cloud; systems but not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Flink streaming systems work, specialized DC audience.
abstract: Dataflow streaming systems, like Apache Flink and Spark Streaming, are integral to modern business analytics, providing real-time insights across industries. However, for emerging hybrid edge-cloud analytics pipelines, neither processing everything in the cloud nor static edge offloading can reliably sustain the target rate under dynamic WAN conditions and limited edge resources. In this paper, we explore how these datacenter-centric platforms can be extended to support such hybrid analytics pipelines. Our goal is to maintain full transparency for user applications, while retaining built-in fault tolerance, out-of-order processing, and existing ecosystem integrations. Achieving this is challenging because existing dataflow engines assume homogeneous resources, rely on static task placement, and do not support adaptation under dynamic network and edge conditions. We introduce Sluice, an adaptive data stream processing system for hybrid clouds, compatible with dataflow streaming engines. Sluice's key contributions are: (i) an automatic query rewriter that decomposes applications into independent, fault-tolerant segments, and (ii) a live routing mechanism that shifts computations between edge and cloud without pausing execution while preserving event-time semantics. We implement Sluice on Apache Flink and evaluate it on a physical testbed with Raspberry Pi devices, as well as on a large simulated testbed of 100 VMs. Across five real-world applications, our results show that Sluice seamlessly shifts computations between edge and cloud, while consistently achieving higher throughput than baseline systems.

title: Video World Models Need Predictable Latents
justification: Video world models with predictable latents; cheaper inference but video gen, not LLM.
hype_justification: World models are hot; Sherry Yang co-author boosts attention.
abstract: Video world models trained on large-scale robot data promise a safe and scalable approach for learning and evaluating policies that act in the physical world. However, they still struggle with long-horizon rollouts and out-of-distribution generalization, and they remain computationally demanding at inference time. Typically, video world models make predictions in the latent space of a reconstruction-trained autoencoder, which however is not directly optimized for dynamics modeling. On the other hand, world models designed for latent planning usually optimize latents to be predictable, but they forgo accurate prediction of observations in pixel space. In this paper, we show that it is possible to achieve the best of both worlds: a latent geometry optimized to make future prediction as simple as possible without sacrificing accurate prediction of future observations. More precisely, we find that temporal objectives for representation learning, paired with a past-conditioned decoder architecture, lead to consistent improvements in generative video world models at the same training budget. The gains include up to 5x cheaper inference, over 7x faster training, and 15-24% lower pixel and perceptual errors out of distribution and over long horizons. Our world models also agree more closely with real-world policy evaluation when using a vision-language model to judge task success from their pixel-space predictions. Overall, our study indicates that temporal predictability is an important design criterion for the latent space of video world models, and provides concrete guidance on how to incorporate it into the training of autoencoders.

title: Agent Memory as Recommendation: Recommender-System Design for Long-Term Memory of LLM Agents
justification: Agent long-term memory as recommendation; serving-cost framing but memory-selection focused.
hype_justification: Agent memory is trendy; strong accuracy/cost claims, moderate interest.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that serve users across many sessions must choose, for every request, the few stored memories that enter a limited context window. This choice largely decides whether the agent answers correctly, and it runs on every request at Web scale. This selection faces three challenges: a large and growing store, a per-request cost budget, and multi-session questions that need all of their evidence. Many memory systems build notes or graphs with hundreds to thousands of LLM calls per history, and each is designed on its own, so it is unclear which component yields the accuracy. These challenges mirror the properties of recommendation, so we formalize agent memory as budgeted slate recommendation, with the request as the user, stored memories as items and the context window as a slate. The formalization places memory systems in one design space of recommender cascades and factorizes accuracy into the completeness that each stage controls. Guided by it, we propose AgentMemRec, which adapts candidate generation, learning to rank and slate construction from recommender systems and selects memories without any LLM call. On multi-session questions of LongMemEval, AgentMemRec outperforms memory and context-selection methods, including A-Mem, HippoRAG 2, DynamicRAG and T-Mem, by 10 to 31 points of accuracy. It matches an LLM reranker that makes 64 calls per query at 3.2 times lower serving cost, and on LoCoMo it outperforms Mem0 and Zep without any LLM call at write time. The factorization attributes the gains to slates that more often hold all of the evidence, so recommender-system design offers an effective and efficient foundation for the long-term memory of LLM agents.

title: Benchmarking Obstacle-Conditioned Safety in Household Robot Navigation
justification: Obstacle-conditioned safety navigation benchmark; robotics, unrelated.
abstract: Safe household navigation requires robots to regulate clearance and speed according to what an obstacle is and how close it is, without unnecessary conservatism. Yet existing evaluations do not test whether semantic safety distinctions are reflected in continuous motion. To that end, we introduce OSMA-Bench, an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark built on spatially matched scenario sets that differ only in obstacle type. We also propose the \emph{Semantic Sensitivity Index} (SSI), which measures whether clearance and distance-dependent speed and smoothness follow the caution ordering of obstacles. Evaluating VLM-based and vision-language-action (VLA) policies on the benchmark, we find that neither consistently adapts its motion to obstacle safety, even with explicit safety prompts. Our analysis shows that the policies can correctly distinguish obstacles by safety relevance but fail to reflect this distinction in the motion parameters or actions they produce. For VLM-based policies, which recognize the obstacle and then generate a navigation program, adding an explicit parameter-inference step between these two stages improves adaptation. These findings expose a gap in \emph{semantic-to-motion grounding}, highlighting the need to translate semantic caution into appropriately safe motion.

title: Curriculum-Guided Acquisition of Hierarchical Task Knowledge from LLM-Generated Experience
justification: Curriculum HTN learning from LLM traces; planning knowledge, not inference systems.
abstract: Hierarchical task knowledge enables efficient problem solving by allowing previously acquired skills to be reused across tasks and problem instances. In this paper, we investigate curriculum-guided acquisition of hierarchical task knowledge in an HTN learning framework. We compare three approaches: online learning during problem solving, human-designed curricula, and an automated curriculum generation procedure that derives learning experiences from verified LLM-generated solution traces. The proposed procedure solves small training problems with an LLM, extracts task accomplishment information, and transforms it into ordered sequences of state-task learning problems for HTN method acquisition. We evaluate the three approaches across multiple planning domains. The results demonstrate that automatically generated curricula recover much of the benefit of expert-designed curricula while substantially reducing the token cost of online hierarchical knowledge acquisition.

title: Exploring perceptual straightness in learned visual representations
justification: Perceptual straightness in visual representations; neuro-vision, unrelated.
hype_justification: Freeman-group vision-science work, moderate niche interest.
abstract: Humans have been shown to use a "straightened" encoding to represent the natural visual world as it evolves in time (Hénaff et al. 2019). In the context of discrete video sequences, "straightened" means that changes between frames follow a more linear path in representation space at progressively deeper levels of processing. While deep convolutional networks are often proposed as models of human visual processing, many do not straighten natural videos. In this paper, we explore the relationship between network architecture, differing types of robustness, biologically-inspired filtering mechanisms, and representational straightness in response to time-varying input; we identify strengths and limitations of straightness as a useful way of evaluating neural network representations. We find that (1) adversarial training leads to straighter representations in both CNN and transformer-based architectures but (2) this effect is task-dependent, not generalizing to tasks such as segmentation and frame-prediction, where straight representations are not favorable for predictions; and nor to other types of robustness. In addition, (3) straighter representations impart temporal stability to class predictions, even for out-of-distribution data. Finally, (4) biologically-inspired elements increase straightness in the early stages of a network, but do not guarantee increased straightness in downstream layers of CNNs. We show that straightness is an easily computed measure of representational robustness and stability, as well as a hallmark of human representations with benefits for computer vision models.

title: AT-AT: Automatic Tool Optimization from Agent Traces
justification: Automatic tool optimization from agent traces; environment-side learning, not inference systems.
hype_justification: MCP tool optimization with enterprise results, timely agent topic.
abstract: Efforts to improve LLM-based agents typically focus on modifying the agent itself, yet success also depends on the environment in which an agent acts. Tools mediate this interaction: a tool's description shapes how an agent calls it, and its implementation determines the results and errors the agent receives afterwards. Many tools, such as APIs and MCP servers, are shared by many agents and maintained by providers who cannot change those agents. We introduce AT-AT (Automatic Tool Optimization from Agent Traces), an agentic tool optimizer that improves a shared toolset offline from historical agent executions while holding the agents fixed. A lightweight coding agent reads agent trajectories and their evaluation results, and selectively edits tool descriptions and, when permitted, implementations. On $τ^2$-bench-verified, AT-AT achieves the highest task completion rates in the Airline and Telecom domains at lower cost than strong prompt- and tool-optimizer baselines, and its Telecom gain is statistically significant under paired permutation tests. Optimizing the tools within a coding agent harness also improves held-out performance on TerminalBench-2 and TBLite. When applied to three production MCP servers at a large enterprise, AT-AT lowered cost or tool error rates on every server and increased held-out task passes on one. By turning accumulated execution traces into updates to shared tool environments, AT-AT provides a path toward continual improvement of agent systems through environment-side learning.

title: Pro-Active Inference
justification: Pro-Active statistical inference for mean estimation; active statistics, unrelated.
hype_justification: Candès-group statistics, cited in that community but off-topic here.
abstract: Estimating a population mean is fundamental across scientific applications, but observing every outcome can be prohibitively expensive. Often, covariates and machine learning (ML) predictions are available for the full population, even when only a small subset of outcomes can be observed. How can we leverage this information to proactively select observations to label, update ML predictions as labels arrive, and construct statistically valid confidence intervals? We develop a general, without-replacement formulation of Pro-Active Inference (PAI), extending our earlier with-replacement approach and building on Active Statistical Inference. Rather than making fixed-order label-skip decisions, PAI proactively selects which observation to label next from the remaining covariate pool while accommodating online ML updates. We establish PAI's finite-sample unbiasedness and asymptotic validity, develop an improved finite-sample variance estimator, and extend PAI to superpopulation inference without Bonferroni corrections or $α$-splitting. We characterize PAI's potential efficiency gains over Batch Active Inference in a quasi-oracle setting, highlighting the role of prediction-residual imbalance.
